## TRANSLATORS' PREFACE

<image-desc>An ornate woodcut initial letter 'F' contained within a square frame decorated with floral and leaf patterns.</image-desc>**FOR** more than a century English speaking students have been placed in the anomalous position of hearing Galileo constantly referred to as the founder of modern physical science, without having any chance to read, in their own language, what Galileo himself has to say. Archimedes has been made available by Heath; <note>Sir Thomas Heath (1861–1940) was a British civil servant and scholar who produced the definitive English translations of ancient Greek mathematics, including the works of Archimedes in 1897.</note> Huygens' *Light* has been turned into English by Thompson, <note>Silvanus P. Thompson (1851–1916) translated Christiaan Huygens' 1690 "Treatise on Light" into English in 1912.</note> while Motte has put the *Principia* of Newton back into the language in which it was conceived. <note>Andrew Motte (1696–1734) published the first English translation of Isaac Newton's Latin masterpiece, the "Philosophiæ Naturalis Principia Mathematica," in 1729.</note> To render the Physics of Galileo also accessible to English and American students is the purpose of the following translation.

The last of the great creators of the Renaissance was not a prophet without honor in his own time; for it was only one group of his country-men that failed to appreciate him. Even during his life time, his *Mechanics* had been rendered into French by one of the leading physicists of the world, Mersenne. <note>Marin Mersenne (1588–1648) was a French monk and mathematician who served as a central hub for scientific correspondence in Europe; he translated Galileo's "Mechanics" in 1634.</note>

Within twenty-five years after the death of Galileo, his *Dialogues on Astronomy*, and those on *Two New Sciences*, had been done into English by Thomas Salusbury and were worthily printed in two handsome quarto volumes. The *Two New Sciences*, which contains practically all that Galileo has to say on the subject of physics, issued from the English press in 1665. <note>Thomas Salusbury’s 1665 translation is famously rare because most copies were destroyed in the Great Fire of London in 1666, making Galileo’s work virtually inaccessible to English readers for centuries.</note>

<summary>In this preface, the translators explain that while Galileo is celebrated as the father of modern physics, his actual writings remained largely inaccessible to English speakers until this edition. They situate the work alongside other translated scientific classics by Newton, Huygens, and Archimedes.</summary>

<keywords>Galileo Galilei, Joseph-Louis Lagrange, Translators' Preface, History of Science, Physics translations, Thomas Salusbury, Marin Mersenne, Scientific Revolution</keywords>

## TRANSLATORS' PREFACE

It is supposed that most of the copies were destroyed in the great London fire which occurred in the year following. <note>The Great Fire of London in 1666 destroyed the city's commercial heart, including many bookshops and publishers' warehouses around St. Paul's Cathedral.</note> We are not aware of any copy in America: even that belonging to the British Museum is an imperfect one.

Again in 1730 the *Two New Sciences* was done into English by Thomas Weston; <note>Thomas Weston (d. 1728) was a mathematics master at the Academy of Greenwich. His translation was published two years after his death.</note> but this book, now nearly two centuries old, is scarce and expensive. Moreover, the literalness with which this translation was made renders many passages either ambiguous or unintelligible to the modern reader. Other than these two, no English version has been made.

Quite recently an eminent Italian scholar, after spending thirty of the best years of his life upon the subject, has brought to completion the great <term>National Edition<gloss>Known in Italian as the "Edizione Nazionale delle opere di Galileo Galilei," this 20-volume set is the definitive collection of Galileo's writings, compiled between 1890 and 1909.</gloss></term> of the Works of Galileo. We refer to the twenty superb volumes in which Professor Antonio Favaro of Padua has given a definitive presentation of the labors of the man who created the modern science of physics.

The following rendition includes neither *The Mechanics* <note>original: "Le Mechaniche"</note> of Galileo nor his paper *On Accelerated Motion* <note>original: "De Motu Accelerato"</note>, since the former of these contains little but the Statics which was current before the time of Galileo, and the latter is essentially included in the Dialogue of the Third Day. Dynamics was the one subject to which under various forms, such as Ballistics, Acoustics, Astronomy, he consistently and persistently devoted his whole life. Into the one volume here translated he seems to have gathered, during his last years, practically all that is of value either to the engineer or the physicist. The historian, the philosopher, and the astronomer will find the other volumes replete with interesting material.

It is hardly necessary to add that we have strictly followed the text of the National Edition—essentially the <term>Elzevir edition<gloss>The original 1638 edition of the "Two New Sciences" published in Leiden, Netherlands. Galileo had to smuggle the manuscript out of Italy because the Inquisition had banned the publication of any of his works.</gloss></term> of 1638. All comments and annotations have been omitted save here and there a foot-note intended to economize the reader’s time. To each of these footnotes has been attached the signature *[Trans.]* in order to preserve the original as nearly intact as possible.

Much of the value of any historical document lies in the language employed, and this is doubly true when one attempts to

## TRANSLATORS' PREFACE

...trace the rise and growth of any set of concepts such as those employed in modern physics. We have therefore made this translation as literal as is consistent with clearness and modernity. In cases where there is any important deviation from this rule, and in the case of many technical terms where there is no deviation from it, we have given the original Italian or Latin phrase in italics enclosed in square brackets. The intention here is to illustrate the great variety of terms employed by the early physicists to describe a single definite idea, and conversely, to illustrate the numerous senses in which, then as now, a single word is used. For the few explanatory English words which are placed in square brackets without italics, the translators alone are responsible. The paging of the <term>National Edition<gloss>The "Edizione Nazionale delle opere di Galileo Galilei," published in 20 volumes between 1890 and 1909, edited by Antonio Favaro.</gloss></term> is indicated in square brackets inserted along the median line of the page.

The imperfections of the following pages would have been many more but for the aid of three of our colleagues. Professor D. R. Curtiss <note>David Raymond Curtiss (1878–1953) was a prominent mathematician at Northwestern University.</note> was kind enough to assist in the translation of those pages which discuss the nature of Infinity: Professor O. H. Basquin <note>Olin Hanson Basquin was a professor of Applied Mechanics at Northwestern University's College of Engineering.</note> gave valuable help in the rendition of the chapter on Strength of Materials; and Professor O. F. Long <note>Orazio Fuortes Long was a Professor of Latin at Northwestern University.</note> cleared up the meaning of a number of Latin phrases.

To Professor A. Favaro <note>Antonio Favaro (1847–1922) was the preeminent Galileo scholar of the late 19th century and director of the National Edition.</note> of the University of Padua the translators share, with every reader, a feeling of sincere obligation for his Introduction.

->H. C.<-
->A. DE S.<-

->EVANSTON, ILLINOIS,<-

# INTRODUCTION

<image-desc>Ornamental drop cap "W" within a square frame. A winged putto or cherub stands to the left of the letter, supporting a shield upon which the "W" is displayed. The background consists of dense horizontal and vertical hatching.</image-desc>

<margin>✓</margin>
Writing to his faithful friend Elia Diodati <note>A Swiss-born jurist who helped circulate Galileo's works in Europe when they were banned in Italy.</note>, Galileo speaks of the “New Sciences” <note>Referring to his 1638 masterpiece, *Discourses and Mathematical Demonstrations Relating to Two New Sciences*.</note> which he had in mind to print as being “superior to everything else of mine hitherto published”; elsewhere he says “they contain results which I consider the most important of all my studies”; and this opinion which he expressed concerning his own work has been confirmed by posterity: the “New Sciences” are, indeed, the masterpiece of Galileo who at the time when he made the above remarks had spent upon them more than thirty laborious years.

<margin>✓</margin>
One who wishes to trace the history of this remarkable work will find that the great philosopher laid its foundations during the eighteen best years of his life—those which he spent at Padua <note>Galileo taught at the University of Padua from 1592 to 1610, a period he described as the happiest of his life.</note>. As we learn from his last scholar, Vincenzio Viviani <note>Galileo’s devoted pupil and first biographer.</note>, the numerous results at which Galileo had arrived while in this city, awakened intense admiration in the friends who had witnessed various experiments by means of which he was accustomed to investigate interesting questions in physics. Fra Paolo Sarpi <note>A Venetian polymath and advisor to the Republic of Venice.</note> exclaimed: To give us the Science of Motion, God and Nature have joined hands and created the intellect of Galileo. And when the “New Sciences” came from the press one of his foremost pupils, Paolo Aproino, wrote that the volume contained much which he had “already heard from his own lips” during student days at Padua.

Limiting ourselves to only the more important documents which might be cited in support of our statement, it will suffice to mention the letter, written to Guidobaldo del Monte <note>An aristocrat and mathematician who was an early patron and friend of Galileo.</note> on the 29th of November, 1602, concerning the descent of heavy bodies <note>This refers to Galileo’s foundational research into gravity and acceleration.</note>

# INTRODUCTION

along the arcs of circles and the chords subtended by them; that to Sarpi <note>Paolo Sarpi (1552–1623), a Venetian polymath and close friend of Galileo who shared his interest in physics and mathematics.</note>, dated 16th of October, 1604, dealing with the free fall of heavy bodies; the letter to Antonio de’ Medici <note>The son of Grand Duke Francesco I of Tuscany.</note> on the 11th of February, 1609, in which he states that he has “completed all the theorems and demonstrations pertaining to forces and resistances of beams of various lengths, thicknesses and shapes, proving that they are weaker at the middle than near the ends, that they can carry a greater load when that load is distributed throughout the length of the beam than when concentrated at one point, demonstrating also what shape should be given to a beam in order that it may have the same bending strength at every point,” and that he was now engaged “upon some questions dealing with the motion of projectiles”; and finally in the letter to Belisario Vinta <note>The Secretary of State to the Grand Duke of Tuscany.</note>, dated 7th of May, 1610, concerning his return from Padua to Florence, he enumerates various pieces of work which were still to be completed, mentioning explicitly three books on an entirely new science dealing with the theory of motion. Although at various times after the return to his native state he devoted considerable thought to the work which, even at that date, he had in mind as is shown by certain fragments which clearly belong to different periods of his life and which have, for the first time, been published in the National Edition <note>The *Edizione Nazionale delle Opere di Galileo Galilei*, the definitive collection of his works edited by Antonio Favaro at the end of the 19th century.</note>; and although these studies were always uppermost in his thought it does not appear that he gave himself seriously to them until after the publication of the *Dialogue* <note>The *Dialogue Concerning the Two Chief World Systems* (1632), which compared the Copernican and Ptolemaic systems.</note> and the completion of that trial which was rightly described as the disgrace of the century <note>Galileo’s 1633 trial by the Roman Inquisition, where he was forced to recant his support for the idea that the Earth moves around the Sun.</note>. In fact as late as October, 1630, he barely mentions to Aggiunti <note>Niccolò Aggiunti, one of Galileo's favorite pupils.</note> his discoveries in the theory of motion, and only two years later, in a letter to Marsili concerning the motion of projectiles, he hints at a book nearly ready for publication in which he will treat also of this subject; and only a year after this he writes to Arrighetti that he has in hand a treatise on the resistance of solids.

But the work was given definite form by Galileo during his enforced residence at Siena: in these five months spent quietly with the Archbishop <note>Ascanio Piccolomini, the Archbishop of Siena, who was a former student and friend of Galileo and provided him with a sanctuary after his condemnation.</note> he himself writes that he has completed “a treatise on a new branch of mechanics full of interesting and useful ideas”; so that a few months later he was able to send

<meta>This page continues the historical narrative of the publication of Galileo’s final masterpiece, *Two New Sciences*. It describes the obstacles placed by the Roman Inquisition and the eventual decision to publish the work in the more liberal atmosphere of the Netherlands.</meta>

->INTRODUCTION<-

word to Micanzio <note>Fulgenzio Micanzio (1570–1654), a Servite monk and theologian in Venice who acted as Galileo’s primary contact and advocate in the Venetian Republic.</note> that the “work was ready”; as soon as his friends learned of this, they urged its publication. It was, however, no easy matter to print the work of a man already condemned by the <term>Holy Office</term> <note>The Roman Inquisition, the department of the Papal government charged with defending Church doctrine and prosecuting heresy.</note>: and since Galileo could not hope to print it either in Florence or in Rome, he turned to the faithful Micanzio asking him to find out whether this would be possible in Venice, from whence he had received offers to print the *Dialogue on the Principal Systems* <note>Referring to the *Dialogue Concerning the Two Chief World Systems* (1632), the book that led to Galileo's trial and house arrest.</note>, as soon as the news had reached there that he was encountering difficulties. At first everything went smoothly; so that Galileo commenced sending to Micanzio some of the manuscript which was received by the latter with an enthusiasm in which he was second to none of the warmest admirers of the great philosopher. But when Micanzio consulted the Inquisitor, he received the answer that there was an express order prohibiting the printing or reprinting of any work of Galileo, either in Venice or in any other place, **with no exception made** <note>original: “nullo excepto”</note>.

As soon as Galileo received this discouraging news he began to look with more favor upon offers which had come to him from Germany where his friend, and perhaps also his scholar, Giovanni Battista Pieroni <note>An Italian military engineer and architect serving the Holy Roman Emperor; he was a devoted former student of Galileo.</note>, was in the service of the Emperor, as military engineer; consequently Galileo gave to Prince Mattia de’ Medici <note>The third son of Grand Duke Cosimo II of Tuscany, who was then serving as a commander in the Thirty Years' War.</note> who was just leaving for Germany the first two Dialogues to be handed to Pieroni who was undecided whether to publish them at Vienna or Prague or at some place in Moravia; in the meantime, however, he had obtained permission to print both at Vienna and at Olmütz. But Galileo recognized danger at every point within reach of the long arm of the Court of Rome; hence, availing himself of the opportunity offered by the arrival of Louis Elzevir <note>A member of the famous Elzevir family of Dutch printers, known for their high-quality editions and for operating outside the reach of the Catholic Inquisition.</note> in Italy in 1636, also of the friendship between the latter and Micanzio, not to mention a visit at Arcetri <note>The village in the hills above Florence where Galileo lived under house arrest.</note>, he decided to abandon all other plans and entrust to the Dutch publisher the printing of his new work the manuscript of which, although not complete, Elzevir took with him on his return home.

xii

->INTRODUCTION<-

<margin>
Through the helpful mediation of Diodati <note>Elia Diodati (1576–1661), a lawyer and friend of Galileo who facilitated the publication of his works in Northern Europe.</note>, the work was offered to the Count of Noailles <note>François de Noailles (1584–1645), the French ambassador to Rome and a former student of Galileo. His diplomatic status provided a layer of protection for the work.</note>, a former student of Galileo’s at Padua. Since 1634, he had served as the French ambassador in Rome and had done much to soften the harsh effects of Galileo's famous trial; the Count accepted the offer with gratitude. The wording of the dedication is worth noting. Because Galileo was well aware that printing his works was strictly forbidden, and because he did not want to anger the Roman authorities—from whom he still hoped to receive a full pardon—he used the dedicatory letter to create a fiction. In this letter (where he only provides a basic outline, likely out of extreme caution), he pretends he had no role in the book's publication. He claims he will never again publish any of his research, and at most would only share handwritten copies here and there. He even acts very surprised that his new *Dialogues* had reached the hands of the Elzevirs <note>The Elzevirs were a renowned Dutch family of printers. Because they operated in the Protestant Netherlands, they were beyond the reach of the Catholic Church’s censorship.</note> and were about to be published. Having been asked to write a dedication, he claims he could think of no one more worthy than the Count, who could also defend him against his detractors on this occasion.
</margin>

Regarding the title, which reads: *Discourses and Mathematical Demonstrations concerning Two New Sciences pertaining to Mechanics and Local Motions*, we only know that this was not the title Galileo himself had planned. In fact, he complained that the publishers took the liberty of changing it, replacing what he called his "noble and dignified" title with one he considered "low and common."

In reprinting this work for the National Edition <note>The *Edizione Nazionale delle Opere di Galileo Galilei*, the definitive 20-volume collection of Galileo's works edited by Antonio Favaro at the end of the 19th century.</note>, I have followed the 1638 Leyden text closely but not blindly. I wanted to use the extensive collection of original manuscripts that have survived to correct many errors found in that first edition. I also wanted to include several additions that the author himself had requested. In the Leyden Edition, the four Dialogues are followed by an “*Appendix containing some theorems and their proofs, dealing with centers of gravity of solid bodies, written by the same Author at an earlier date*.” This section has no direct link to the topics discussed in the Dialogues; Galileo mentions that he discovered these theorems "at the age of twenty-two and...

It also notes Galileo's dissatisfaction with the title chosen by his publishers and the editorial methods used in later scholarly editions.</summary>

# INTRODUCTION

But it was not the intention of Galileo that the *Dialogues on the New Sciences* should contain only the four Days and the above-mentioned appendix which constitute the Leyden <note>Leyden, now spelled Leiden, is a city in the Netherlands where the Elzevir press was located; it was a center for academic publishing outside the reach of the Roman Inquisition.</note> Edition; while, on the one hand, the Elzevirs <note>The Elzevirs were a famous family of Dutch booksellers and printers who published Galileo's work when it was banned in Italy.</note> were hastening the printing and striving to complete it at the earliest possible date, Galileo, on the other hand, kept on speaking of another Day <note>Galileo organized his "New Sciences" as a series of conversations (Dialogues) taking place over several "Days."</note>, besides the four, thus embarrassing and perplexing the printers. From the correspondence which went on between author and publisher, it appears that this Fifth Day was to have treated “of the force of percussion <term>percussion [the physics of the force exerted by a body in motion when it strikes another body]</term> and the use of the catenary <term>catenary [the curve formed by a chain or cable hanging freely from two points]</term>”; but as the typographical work approached completion, the printer became anxious for the book to issue from the press without further delay; and thus it came to pass that the *Discourses and Demonstrations* <note>original: "*Discorsi e Dimostrazioni*"</note> appeared containing only the four Days and the Appendix, in spite of the fact that in April, 1638, Galileo had plunged more deeply than ever “into the profound question of percussion” and “had almost reached a complete solution.”

The “New Sciences” now appear in an edition following the text which I, after the most careful and devoted study, determined upon for the National Edition <note>The National Edition (*Edizione Nazionale*) is the standard, scholarly 20-volume collection of Galileo’s entire body of work, compiled and edited by Antonio Favaro.</note>. It appears also in that language in which, above all others, I have desired to see it. In this translation, the last and ripest work of the great philosopher makes its first appearance in the New World: if toward this important result I may hope to have contributed in some measure I shall feel amply rewarded for having given to this field of research the best years of my life.

The fact of your carrying them to France and showing them to friends of yours who are skilled in these sciences gave evidence that my silence was not to be interpreted as complete idleness. A little later, just as I was on the point of [44] sending other copies to Germany, Flanders, England, Spain and possibly to some places in Italy, I was notified by the **Elzevirs** <note>The Elzevir family were famous Dutch printers and publishers known for their high-quality editions of scientific and classical works.</note> that they had these works of mine in press and that I ought to decide upon a dedication and send them a reply at once. It is, therefore, proper that I dedicate to your Lordship this child of my brain. To this course I am constrained not only by the weight of obligation under which you have placed me, but also, if I may so speak, by the interest which I have in securing your Lordship as the defender of my reputation against adversaries <note>Galileo is likely referring to the ecclesiastical authorities and conservative scholars who opposed his heliocentric views and scientific methods.</note> who may attack it while I remain under your protection.

And now, advancing under your banner, I pay my respects to you by wishing that you may be rewarded for these kindnesses by the achievement of the highest happiness and greatness.

SINCE society is held together by the mutual services which men render one to another, and since to this end the <term>arts and sciences</term> <note>In the 17th century, "arts" referred to practical skills or crafts, while "sciences" referred to theoretical knowledge.</note> have largely contributed, investigations in these fields have always been held in great esteem and have been highly regarded by our wise forefathers. The larger the utility and excellence of the inventions, the greater has been the honor and praise bestowed upon the inventors. Indeed, men have even deified them and have united in the attempt to perpetuate the memory of their benefactors by the bestowal of this supreme honor.

Praise and admiration are likewise due to those clever intellects who, confining their attention to the known, have discovered and corrected fallacies and errors in many and many a proposition enunciated by men of distinction and accepted for ages as fact. Although these men have only pointed out falsehood and have not replaced it by truth, they are nevertheless worthy of commendation when we consider the well-known difficulty of discovering fact—a difficulty which led the <term>prince of orators</term> <note>A traditional reference to the Roman statesman and philosopher Cicero.</note> to exclaim: *I wish that I could as easily discover the truth as I can expose falsehood.* <note>original Latin: "Utinam tam facile possem vera reperire, quam falsa convincere." from Cicero, *On the Nature of the Gods* (De Natura Deorum), Book I, section 91.</note>

...unanimous approval of scholars assign the first place to Galileo Galilei, Member of the <term>Academy of the Lincei</term> <note>The "Academy of the Lynxes," founded in 1603, was one of the first scientific societies in the world. Remembering that the wisdom and power and goodness of the Creator are nowhere exhibited so well as in the heavens and celestial bodies, we can easily recognize the great merit of him who has brought these bodies to our knowledge and has, in spite of their almost infinite distance, rendered them easily visible. For, according to the common saying, sight can teach more and with greater certainty in a single day than can <term>precept</term> <note>Formal rules or theoretical instructions.</note> even though repeated a thousand times; or, as another says, intuitive knowledge keeps pace with accurate definition.

But the divine and natural gifts of this man are shown to best advantage in the present work where he is seen to have discovered, though not without many labors and long vigils, two entirely new sciences and to have demonstrated them in a rigid, that is, geometric, manner: and what is even more remarkable in this work is the fact that one of the two sciences deals with a subject of never-ending interest, perhaps the most important in nature, one which has engaged the minds of all the great philosophers and one concerning which an extraordinary number of books have been written. I refer to motion <insert>local motion</insert> <note>original: "moto locale"; this refers to the physics of objects moving through space.</note>, a phenomenon exhibiting very many wonderful properties, none of which has hitherto been discovered or demonstrated by any one. # FIRST DAY

## INTERLOCUTORS: SALVIATI, SA-
## GREDO AND SIMPLICIO
<note>Galileo presents his scientific arguments through three fictionalized characters: Salviati represents Galileo’s own groundbreaking views; Sagredo is the intelligent, open-minded host; and Simplicio represents the traditional, often flawed, Aristotelian worldview of the time.</note>

SALV. The constant activity which you Venetians display in your famous arsenal <note>The Venetian Arsenal was a vast complex of shipyards and armories that served as the industrial heart of Venice; it was an ideal setting for Galileo to study the intersection of practical engineering and theoretical science.</note> suggests to the studious mind a large field for investigation, especially that part of the work which involves <term>mechanics</term> <note>In the 17th century, "mechanics" referred to the study of machines and the practical application of mathematical principles to physical tools.</note>; for in this department all types of instruments and machines are constantly being constructed by many artisans, among whom there must be some who, partly by inherited experience and partly by their own observations, have become highly expert and clever in explanation.

SAGR. You are quite right. Indeed, I myself, being curious by nature, frequently visit this place for the mere pleasure of observing the work of those who, on account of their superiority over other artisans, we call "first rank men." Conference with them has often helped me in the investigation of certain effects including not only those which are striking, but also those which are <term>recondite</term> <note>Hidden, obscure, or difficult to understand.</note> and almost incredible. At times also I have been put to confusion and driven to despair of ever explaining something for which I could not account, but which my senses told me to be true. And notwithstanding the fact that what the old man told us a little while ago is proverbial and commonly accepted, yet it seemed to me altogether false, like many another saying which is current among the ignorant; for I think they introduce these expressions in order to give the appearance of knowing something about matters which they do not understand.

<summary>The dialogue opens at the Venetian Arsenal, where the characters reflect on how the practical expertise of skilled craftsmen can provide deep insights into the laws of physics and mechanics.</summary>

--- Page 36 ---
<meta>catchword: did. This page continues the conversation from the Venetian Arsenal. Having established the setting, the characters now begin to debate the "Square-Cube Law"—the idea that physical structures do not scale linearly in strength as they increase in size.</meta>

# THE TWO NEW SCIENCES OF GALILEO

->[50]<-

SALV. You refer, perhaps, to that last remark of his <note>Referring to the expert shipbuilder at the Arsenal mentioned on the previous page.</note> when we asked the reason why they employed stocks, scaffolding and bracing of larger dimensions for launching a big vessel than they do for a small one; and he answered that they did this in order to avoid the danger of the ship parting under its own **huge weight** <note>original: "*vasta mole*"</note>, a danger to which small boats are not subject?

<margin>A pencil checkmark and vertical bracket mark the second half of this paragraph in the source text.</margin>
SAGR. Yes, that is what I mean; and I refer especially to his last assertion which I have always regarded as a false, though current, opinion; namely, that in speaking of these and other similar machines one cannot argue from the small to the large, because many devices which succeed on a small scale do not work on a large scale. Now, since **mechanics** <note>The mathematical study of motion and the forces that produce it.</note> has its foundation in **geometry**, where mere size cuts no figure, I do not see that the properties of circles, triangles, cylinders, cones and other solid figures will change with their size. If, therefore, a large machine be constructed in such a way that its parts bear to one another the same ratio as in a smaller one, and if the smaller is sufficiently strong for the purpose for which it was designed, I do not see why the larger also should not be able to withstand any severe and destructive tests to which it may be subjected.

SALV. The common opinion is here absolutely wrong. Indeed, it is so far wrong that precisely the opposite is true, namely, that many machines can be constructed even more perfectly on a large scale than on a small; thus, for instance, a clock which indicates and strikes the hour can be made more accurate on a large scale than on a small. A large marble column was laid out so that its two ends rested each upon a piece of beam; a little later it occurred to a <term>mechanic</term><note>original: "artefice"; in Galileo’s time, this referred to a skilled craftsman, engineer, or master builder.</note> that, in order to be doubly sure of its not breaking in the middle by its own weight, it would be wise to lay a third support midway. But in the case of the rope the very act of twisting causes the threads to bind one another in such a way that when the rope is stretched with a great force the fibres break rather than separate from each other.

At the point where a rope parts the fibres are, as everyone knows, very short, nothing like a <term>cubit</term> long, as they would be if the parting of the rope occurred, not by the breaking of the filaments, but by their slipping one over the other.

**SAGREDO:** In confirmation of this it may be remarked that ropes sometimes break not by a lengthwise pull but by excessive twisting. This, it seems to me, is a conclusive argument because the threads bind one another so tightly that the compressing fibres do not permit those which are compressed to lengthen the spirals even that little bit by which it is necessary for them to lengthen in order to surround the rope which, on twisting, grows shorter and thicker.

**SALVIATI:** You are quite right. Now see how one fact suggests another.

**SALVIATI.** A truly ingenious device! I feel, however, that for a complete explanation other considerations might well enter; yet I must not now digress upon this particular topic since you are waiting to hear what I think about the **breaking strength** of other materials which, unlike ropes and most woods, do not show a **filamentous structure** <term>filamentous structure<note>A material made of long, thread-like fibers (like hemp or wood grain) woven or bundled together.</note></term>. The **coherence** <note>The internal "stickiness" or force that holds the parts of a solid object together.</note> of these bodies is, in my estimation, produced by other causes which may be grouped under two heads. One is that much-talked-of **repugnance which nature exhibits towards a vacuum** <note>Often called "horror vacui," this was the traditional Aristotelian belief that nature "abhors" empty space and will exert force to prevent a vacuum from forming.</note>; but this horror of a vacuum not being sufficient, it is necessary to introduce another cause in the form of a gluey or viscous substance which binds firmly together the component parts of the body.

First I shall speak of the vacuum, demonstrating by definite experiment the quality and quantity of its **force** <note>original: *virtù*</note>. If you take two highly polished and smooth plates of marble, metal, or glass and place them face to face, one will slide over the other with the greatest ease, showing conclusively that there is nothing of a viscous or gluey nature between them. But when you attempt to separate them and keep them at a constant distance apart, you find the plates exhibit such a repugnance to separation that the upper one will carry the lower one with it and keep it lifted indefinitely, even when the latter is big and heavy.

This experiment shows the aversion of nature for empty space, even during the brief moment required for the outside air to rush in and fill up the region between the two plates. It is also observed that if two plates are not thoroughly polished, their contact is imperfect so that when you attempt to separate them slowly the only resistance offered is that of weight; if, however, the pull be sudden, then the lower plate rises, but quickly falls back, having followed the upper plate only for that very short interval of time required for the expansion of the small amount of air remaining between the plates, in consequence of their not fitting, and for the entrance of the surrounding air. This resistance which is exhibited between the two

**SAGREDO.** Allow me to interrupt you for a moment, please; for I want to speak of something which just occurs to me. When I see how the lower plate follows the upper one and how rapidly it is lifted, I feel sure that—contrary to the opinion of many philosophers, including perhaps even **Aristotle** himself—**motion in a vacuum is not instantaneous**. 

If motion in a vacuum were instantaneous, the two plates mentioned above would separate without any resistance whatever, because the same instant of time would be enough for them to pull apart and for the surrounding air to rush in and fill the empty space between them. The fact that the lower plate follows the upper one allows us to infer two things: first, that motion in a vacuum is not instantaneous; and second, that a **vacuum** <note>An empty space containing no matter at all.</note> really exists between the two plates, at least for a very short time—just long enough to allow the surrounding air to rush in and fill the gap. If there were no vacuum created, there would be no need for the surrounding air to move at all. We must admit, then, that a vacuum is sometimes produced by **violent motion** <term>violent motion<note>original: *violenza*. In the physics of this era, "natural motion" was an object's tendency to move to its natural place (like a stone falling), while "violent motion" was any movement caused by an external force.</note></term> or contrary to the laws of nature (although, in my opinion, nothing occurs "contrary to nature" except the impossible, and the impossible never happens).

But here another difficulty arises. While the experiment convinces me this conclusion is correct, my mind is not entirely satisfied as to the cause. The separation of the plates happens *before* the vacuum is formed as a result of that separation. In the order of nature, a cause must come before its effect (even if they seem to happen at the same time). Since every real effect must have a real cause, I do not see how the sticking together of the plates and their resistance to being pulled apart—which are actual facts—can be blamed on a vacuum that hasn't even happened yet. According to the infallible maxim of **the Philosopher** <note>A common title for Aristotle in the Renaissance.</note>, "that which does not exist can produce no effect" <note>original: *non-entis nulla sunt accidentia*. A standard logical rule: a thing that doesn't exist cannot have properties or cause things to happen.</note>.

<summary>Sagredo challenges the Aristotelian idea that motion in a vacuum is instantaneous, using the example of two suctioned plates. He also raises a philosophical paradox: how can a vacuum that is "about to form" be the cause of the plates currently sticking together?</summary>

Once we have reached this point, let us see how easy it is to calculate the maximum length to which cylinders of metal, stone, wood, or glass of any thickness can be stretched before they break under their own weight.

->[65]<-

Take, for example, a copper wire of any length and thickness. Fix the upper end and attach heavier and heavier loads to the other end until it finally snaps. Let us say the maximum load is fifty pounds. It is then clear that if fifty pounds of copper—plus the weight of the wire itself (which might be, say, 1/8 of an ounce)—were drawn out into a wire of this same thickness, we would have the maximum length of this kind of wire that can support its own weight. Suppose the wire that breaks is one cubit long and weighs 1/8 of an ounce. Since it supports 50 pounds in addition to its own weight (which is 4,800 eighths-of-an-ounce), it follows that all copper wires, regardless of their size, can only support themselves up to a length of 4,801 cubits and no further. Since a copper rod can hold its own weight up to a length of 4,801 cubits, it follows that the part of the <term>breaking strength</term> <note>original: "resistenza"</note> that depends upon the vacuum—when compared with the other factors of resistance—is equal to the weight of a rod of water eighteen cubits long and as thick as the copper rod. <meta>This page continues Salviati’s explanation of the "Aristotle’s Wheel" paradox. Having established the starting positions of the two nested hexagons (one large, one small), he now describes the mechanics of a single rotation to show how the smaller shape "jumps" across its path to keep pace with the larger one.</meta>

# THE TWO NEW SCIENCES OF GALILEO

### FIRST DAY

...at the same time, the side **IK** moves into the position **OP**. Meanwhile, the center **G** has traveled along a path above the line **GV**, and it does not return to that line until it has completed the **arc** <term>arc: a segment of a circle or a curved line.</term> **GC**. Once this step is finished, the larger polygon comes to rest with its side **BC** lying flat against the line **BQ**. Simultaneously, the side **IK** of the smaller polygon is made to align with the line **OP**, having passed over the segment **IO** without actually touching it. The center **G** will have reached the position **C** after traveling its entire course above the parallel line **GV**. 

Finally, the entire figure will return to a position similar to the one it started in. If we continue the **rotation** <term>rotation: the act of turning around a central point.</term> and proceed to the next step, side **DC** of the larger polygon will land on the segment **QX**. The side **KL** of the smaller polygon—after first skipping the arc **PY**—will fall on **YZ**. During this, the center **G**, still staying above the line **GV**, will return to it at point **R** after leaping over the gap **CR**. 

By the end of one full rotation, the larger polygon will have traced six lines upon the line **AS** without any breaks; these six lines together equal its total **perimeter** <term>perimeter: the total distance around the outside edge of a shape.</term>. The smaller polygon will likewise have marked out six lines equal to its own perimeter, but these are separated by five gaps (arcs). The **chords** <term>chord: a straight line segment connecting two points on a curve.</term> of these arcs represent the parts of the line **HT** that the smaller polygon never touched. The center **G** only touches the line **GV** at six specific points. 

From this, it is clear that the total distance covered by the smaller polygon is almost equal to that covered by the larger one—that is, the line **HT** is nearly as long as the line **AS**. They differ only by the length of one chord of one of these arcs, provided we understand the total length of line **HT** to include those five skipped gaps.

Now, this explanation which I have given using hexagons must be understood to apply to all other **polygons** <term>polygon: a flat geometric shape with at least three straight sides and angles.</term>, regardless of how many sides they have. This holds true as long as they are <note>[70]</note> similar, **concentric** <term>concentric: shapes that share the same center point.</term>, and rigidly connected, so that when the larger one rotates, the smaller one must also turn, no matter how tiny it may be. You must also understand that the lines traced by these two shapes are nearly equal, provided we include in the space traveled by the smaller one those intervals which were never touched by any part of its perimeter.

# THE TWO NEW SCIENCES OF GALILEO

### FIRST DAY

Imagine a large **polygon** <term>polygon: a flat geometric shape with at least three straight sides and angles.</term> of, say, one thousand sides. Let it make one complete **rotation** <term>rotation: the act of turning around a center point or axis.</term> and thus lay off a line equal to its **perimeter** <term>perimeter: the total distance around the outside edge of a shape.</term>. At the same time, the smaller polygon nested inside it will pass over an approximately equal distance. This path is made up of a thousand small portions, each equal to one of its sides, but interrupted by a thousand spaces. In contrast with the portions that touch the ground, we may call these gaps empty. So far, the matter is free from difficulty or doubt.

But now suppose that around any center, let us call it **A**, we describe two **concentric** <term>concentric: circles of different sizes that share the exact same center point, like a bullseye.</term> and rigidly connected circles. Suppose that from the points **C** and **B** on their **radii** <term>radius (plural radii): the distance from the center of a circle to its outer edge.</term>, there are drawn the **tangents** <term>tangent: a straight line that touches the curve of a circle at only one point without crossing through it.</term> **CE** and **BF**, and that through the center **A** the line **AD** is drawn parallel to them. 

Now, if the large circle makes one complete rotation along the line **BF**, it covers a distance equal not only to its own **circumference** <term>circumference: the total distance around the outer edge of a circle.</term> but also to the other two lines, **CE** and **AD**. Tell me, then, what will the smaller circle do, and what will the center do? As for the center, it will certainly travel across and touch every point of the line **AD**. Meanwhile, the circumference of the smaller circle will have measured off by its points of contact the entire line **CE**, just as the polygons did before. 

The only difference is that [on the previous page] the line **HT** was not in contact with the perimeter of the smaller polygon at every point; there were as many vacant spaces left untouched as there were sides. But here, in the case of the circles, the circumference of the smaller one never leaves the line **CE**. No part of the line is left untouched, and there is never a time when some point on the circle is not in contact with the straight line. How, then, can the smaller circle traverse a length greater than its own circumference unless it moves by "jumps"?

**SAGREDO**: It seems to me that one might say that just as the center of the circle is only a single point yet stays in constant contact with the line **AD** as it is carried along, so the points on the circumference of the smaller circle—carried by the motion of the larger circle—might simply slide over certain parts of the line **CE**.

->[71]<-

**SALVIATI**: There are two reasons why this cannot happen. First—

**SAGR.** This is a very intricate matter. I see no solution. Pray explain it to us.

Now this which has been said concerning simple lines must be understood to hold also in the case of surfaces and solid bodies, it being assumed that they are made up of an infinite, not a finite, number of atoms <term>atoms: from the Greek 'atomos,' meaning indivisible; Galileo uses this to describe the ultimate, smallest building blocks of matter.</term>. Thus one can easily imagine a small ball of gold expanded into a very large space without the introduction of a finite number of empty spaces, always provided the gold is made up of an infinite number of indivisible parts.

<meta>This page continues the dialogue between Salviati, Simplicio, and Sagredo. ### FIRST DAY

One of the main objections urged against this building up of **continuous quantities out of indivisibles** <note>original: "continuo d' indivisibili"</note> is that the addition of one indivisible to another cannot produce a divisible, for if this were so it would render the indivisible divisible. Thus if two indivisibles, say two points, can be united to form a quantity, say a divisible line, then an even more divisible line might be formed by the union of three, five, seven, or any other odd number of points. Since however these lines can be cut into two equal parts, it becomes possible to cut the indivisible which lies exactly in the middle of the line. <note>This logical trap suggests that if a line is made of an odd number of points, the middle point would have to be split in half to divide the line equally, which contradicts the definition of a point as "indivisible."</note> In answer to this and other objections of the same type we reply that a divisible magnitude cannot be constructed out of two or ten or a hundred or a thousand indivisibles, but requires an infinite number of them.

**SIMP.** Here a difficulty presents itself which appears to me insoluble. Since it is clear that we may have one line greater than another, each containing an infinite number of points, we are forced to admit that, within one and the same class, we may have something greater than infinity, because the infinity of points in the long line is greater than the infinity of points in the short line. This assigning to an infinite quantity a value greater than infinity is quite beyond my comprehension.

**SALV.** This is one of the difficulties which arise when we attempt, with our finite minds, to discuss the infinite, assigning to it those properties which we give to the finite and limited; but <insert>[78]</insert> <note>Page 78 of the 1890 National Edition of Galileo's works.</note> this I think is wrong, for we cannot speak of infinite quantities as being the one greater or less than or equal to another. To prove this I have in mind an argument which, for the sake of clearness, I shall put in the form of questions to Simplicio who raised this difficulty.

I take it for granted that you know which of the numbers are **squares** <term>square numbers: the product of a whole number multiplied by itself, such as 2 × 2 = 4</term> and which are not.

**SIMP.** I am quite aware that a squared number is one which results from the multiplication of another number by itself; thus 4, 9, etc., are squared numbers which come from multiplying 2, 3, etc., by themselves.

**SALV.** Very well; and you also know that just as the products are called **squares** so the factors are called **sides** or **roots**; <note>Galileo is thinking geometrically: the "root" is the "side" of a square area.</note> while on the other hand those numbers which do not consist of two equal factors are not squares. **SALV.** If I should ask further how many squares there are one might reply truly that there are as many as the corresponding number of roots, since every square has its own root and every root its own square, while no square has more than one root and no root more than one square.

...light, even if not instantaneous, is at least extraordinarily fast. For when we see artillery fired at a great distance, the flash reaches our eyes long before the sound reaches our ears. This fact, considering that the speed of **sound** is as high as it is, assures us that the motion of light cannot fail to be extraordinarily swift. The experiment which I devised was as follows:

Let each of two persons take a light contained in a lantern, or other receptacle, such that by the interposition of the hand, the one can shut off or admit the light to the vision of the other. Next let them stand **opposite** each other at a distance of a few **cubits** <term>Cubit: An ancient unit of length based on the distance from the elbow to the tip of the middle finger, approximately 18 inches or 45 centimeters.</term> and practice until they acquire such skill in uncovering and **occulting** <term>Occulting: The act of hiding or blocking a light source from view.</term> their lights that the instant one sees the light of his companion he will uncover his own. After a few trials the response will be so prompt that without sensible error <note>original: "svario", meaning a slight variation or discrepancy in timing.</note> the uncovering of one light is immediately followed by the uncovering of the other, so that as soon as one exposes his light he will instantly see that of the other. 

Having acquired skill at this short distance let the two experimenters, equipped as before, take up positions separated by a distance of two or three miles and let them perform the same experiment at night, noting carefully whether the exposures and occultations occur in the same manner as at short distances; if they do, we may safely conclude that the **propagation** <term>Propagation: The movement or transmission of light through space.</term> of light is instantaneous; but if time is required at a distance of three miles which, considering the going of one light and the coming of the other, really amounts to six, then the delay ought to be easily observable. If the experiment is to be made at still greater distances, say eight or ten miles, **telescopes** may be employed, each observer adjusting one for himself at the place where he is to make the experiment at night; then although the lights are not large and are therefore invisible to the naked eye at so great a distance, they can readily be covered and uncovered since by aid of the telescopes, once adjusted and fixed, they will become easily visible.

**SAGR.** This experiment strikes me as a clever and reliable invention. But tell us what you conclude from the results.

And first, just as we explained expansion by using the line described by a small circle rotating inside a large one—where the large circle traces a line longer than the circumference of the small one—so, in order to explain contraction, we point out that during each rotation of a smaller circle, the larger one describes a straight line which is shorter than its own circumference.

For a better understanding of this, let us consider what happens in the case of polygons. Using

<insert>[94]</insert>

a figure similar to the earlier one, construct two hexagons, ABC and HIK, around a common center L, and let them roll along the parallel lines HOM and AB*c*. Now, holding the vertex I fixed, allow the smaller polygon to rotate until the side IK lies upon the parallel line; during this motion, point K will describe the arc KM, and the side KI will coincide with the segment IM. Let us see what, in the meantime, the side CB of the larger polygon has been doing. Since the rotation is centered on point I, the terminal point B of the line IB will move backwards, describing the arc B*b* underneath the parallel line *c*A. Thus, when the side KI finally matches the line MI, the side BC will coincide with *bc*. It has advanced only the distance B*c*, having effectively retreated through a portion of the line BA which stays behind the arc B*b*. If we allow the smaller polygon to continue rotating, it will eventually traverse a line equal to its entire perimeter; meanwhile, the larger one will traverse a line *less* than its perimeter by as many times the length *b*B as there are sides.

<margin>[95]</margin>

In the case of the polygons, the point *I* remained fixed until the side *KI* coincided with *MI* and the line *IB* carried the terminal point *B* backward as far as *b*, so that the side *BC* fell upon *bc*. This resulted in <term>superposing</term> <note>Superposition refers to the overlapping of parts of the line, where the larger circle "jumps" back or covers the same ground twice to stay in sync with the smaller circle.</note> upon the line *BA* the portion *Bb*, and advancing by an amount *Bc*, equal to *MI*—that is, to one side of the smaller polygon. 

On account of these superpositions, which represent the amount by which the sides of the larger polygon exceed those of the smaller, each net advance is equal to one side of the smaller polygon. During one complete <term>rotation</term>, these advances amount to a straight line equal in length to the <term>perimeter</term> <note>The total distance around the outside of a shape; for a circle, this is the circumference.</note> of the smaller polygon.

<meta>This page continues Salviati’s explanation of the "Wheel of Aristotle" paradox. Having established how polygons move, he now applies the logic to circles, treating them as polygons with an infinite number of sides to explain how two different-sized wheels can cover the same distance.</meta>

# FIRST DAY

But now reasoning in the same way concerning the circles, we must observe that whereas the number of sides in any polygon is comprised within a certain limit, the number of sides in a circle is infinite; the former are finite and divisible; the latter infinite and **indivisible**. <note>Galileo is employing an early form of calculus-style reasoning, suggesting that a circle is simply a polygon with an infinite number of microscopic sides.</note> In the case of the polygon, the vertices remain at rest during an interval of time which bears to the period of one complete rotation the same ratio which one side bears to the perimeter; likewise, in the case of the circles, the delay of each of the infinite number of vertices is merely instantaneous, because an instant is such a fraction of a finite interval as a point is of a line which contains an infinite number of points.

The retrogression <note>The backward motion occurring at the point of contact.</note> of the sides of the larger polygon is not equal to the length of one of its sides but merely to the excess of such a side over one side of the smaller polygon, the net advance being equal to this smaller side; but in the circle, the point or side *C*, during the instantaneous rest of *B*, recedes by an amount equal to its excess over the side *B*, making a net progress equal to *B* itself. In short the infinite number of **indivisible sides** of the greater circle with their infinite number of infinite retrogressions, made during the infinite number of instantaneous delays of the infinite number of vertices of the smaller circle, together with the infinite number of progressions, equal to the infinite number of sides in the smaller circle—all these, I say, add up to a line equal to that described by the smaller circle, a line which contains an infinite number of infinitely small superpositions, thus bringing about a thickening or contraction without any overlapping or interpenetration of finite parts. You will find, upon observation, a thousand such expansions for they are more obvious than contractions since dense matter is more palpable and accessible to our senses. But without going into the matter more deeply, how have these common and 
<note>[112]</note>
obvious properties escaped your notice? Have you not observed that two bodies which fall in water, one with a speed a hundred times as great as that of the other, will fall in air with speeds so nearly equal that one will not surpass the other by as much as one hundredth part? Thus, for example, an egg made of marble will descend in water one hundred times more rapidly than a hen’s egg, while in air falling from a height of twenty <term>cubits</term> <note>An ancient unit of length based on the distance from the elbow to the tip of the middle finger, roughly 18-20 inches.</note> the one will fall short of the other by less than four finger-breadths. And here, I am sure, Simplicio, you find no ground for difference or objection. We conclude, therefore, that the argument does not bear against the existence of a vacuum; but if it did, it would only do away with vacua of considerable size which neither I nor, in my opinion, the ancients ever believed to exist in nature, although they might possibly be produced by force [*violenza*] <note>original: *violenza* — This refers to "violent motion" or external force applied against the natural tendency of an object.</note> as may be gathered from various experiments whose description would here occupy too much time.

->[113]<-

**SALVIATI.** <note>Salviati is the character who speaks for Galileo himself, presenting his "New Sciences."</note> These are interesting questions, and I have thought much concerning them. I will give you my method of approach and the result which I finally reached. Having once established the falsity of the idea that a body moving through different media acquires speeds inversely proportional to the resistances—and having also disproved the statement that in the same medium, bodies of different weight acquire speeds proportional to their weights—I then began to combine these two facts. 

I considered what would happen if bodies of different weight were placed in media of different resistances. I found that the differences in speed were greater in those media which were more resistant—that is, less yielding. This difference was so significant that two bodies which differed scarcely at all in their speed through air would, in water, fall with one having a speed ten times as great as the other. Furthermore, there are bodies which will fall rapidly in air, whereas if placed in water, they will not only not sink, but will remain at rest or even rise to the top. For example, it is possible to find some kinds of wood, such as knots and roots, which remain suspended in water but fall rapidly in air.

### FIRST DAY

I am convinced that, if the medium <note>In physics, a "medium" is any substance (like air or water) that an object moves through.</note> were entirely removed, the advantage received by the bladder <note>A dried animal bladder was often used in early physics experiments because it is very light and holds a large volume of air, making it highly susceptible to air resistance.</note> would be so great and that coming to the lead so small that their speeds would be equalized. Assuming this principle, that all falling bodies acquire equal speeds in a medium which, on account of a **vacuum** or something else, offers no resistance to the speed of the motion, we shall be able accordingly to determine the ratios of the speeds of both similar and dissimilar bodies moving either through one and the same medium or through different space-filling, and therefore resistant, media. 

This result we may obtain by observing how much the weight of the medium detracts from the weight of the moving body, which weight is the means employed by the falling body to open a path for itself and to push aside the parts of the medium, something which does not happen in a **vacuum** where, therefore, no difference of speed is to be expected from a difference of **specific gravity** <term>specific gravity: the density of a substance compared to a reference substance, such as water or air</term>. And since it is known that the effect of the medium is to diminish the weight of the body by the weight of the medium displaced, we may accomplish our purpose by diminishing in just this proportion the speeds of the **falling bodies**, which in a non-resisting medium we have assumed to be equal.

Thus, for example, imagine lead to be ten thousand times as heavy as air while **ebony** <term>ebony: a very dense, heavy black wood</term> is only one thousand times as heavy.

->[120]<-

Here we have two substances whose speeds of fall in a medium devoid of **resistance** are equal: but, when air is the **medium**, it will subtract from the speed of the lead one part in ten thousand, and from the speed of the ebony one part in one thousand, i. e. ten parts in ten thousand. While therefore lead and ebony would fall from any given height in the same interval of time, provided the retarding effect of the air were removed, the lead will, in air, lose in speed one part in ten thousand; and the ebony, ten parts in ten thousand. In other words, if the elevation from which the bodies start be divided into ten thousand parts, the lead will reach the ground leaving the ebony behind by as much as ten, or at least nine, of these parts. Is it not clear then that a leaden ball allowed to fall from a tower two hundred cubits <note>original: "cubiti". A cubit is an ancient unit of length based on the distance from the elbow to the tip of the middle finger.</note>...

As to the other question, namely, how to determine the **specific gravity** <term>specific gravity: the density of a substance compared to the density of water</term> of air, I have employed the following method. I took a rather large glass bottle with a narrow neck and attached to it a leather cover, binding it tightly about the neck of the bottle: in the top of this cover I inserted and firmly fastened the valve of a leather bottle, through which I forced into the glass bottle, by means of a syringe, a large quantity of air. And since air is easily condensed one can pump into the bottle two or three times its own volume of air. After this I took an accurate balance and weighed this bottle of compressed air with the utmost precision, adjusting the weight with fine sand. I next opened the valve and allowed the compressed air to escape; then replaced the flask upon the balance and found it perceptibly lighter: from the sand which had been used as a counterweight I now removed and laid aside as much as was necessary to again secure balance. 

Under these conditions there can be no doubt but that the weight of the sand thus laid aside represents the weight of the air which had been forced into the flask and had afterwards escaped. But after all this experiment tells me merely that the weight of the compressed air is the same as that of the sand removed from the balance; when however it comes to knowing certainly and definitely the weight of air as compared with that of water or any other heavy substance this I cannot hope to do without first measuring the **volume** <note>original: "quantità"; while this literally translates to "quantity," Galileo is using it here in the scientific sense of volume or the space occupied by the air.</note> of compressed air; for this measurement I have devised the two following methods.

This second flask is provided with a hole in the bottom through which an iron rod can be placed so as to open, at will, the valve above mentioned and thus permit the surplus air of the first to escape after it has once been weighed: but this second bottle must be filled with water. **SALV.** The experiment made to ascertain whether two bodies, differing greatly in weight, will fall from a given height with the same speed offers some difficulty; because, if the height is considerable, the retarding effect of the <term>medium<note>The substance—such as air or water—through which an object moves.</note></term>, which must be penetrated and thrust aside by the falling body, will be greater in the case of the small momentum of the very light body than in the case of the great force <note>original: *violenza*</note> of the heavy body; so that, in a long distance, the light body will be left behind; if the height be small, one may well doubt whether there is any difference; and if there be a difference it will be inappreciable.

It occurred to me therefore to repeat many times the fall through a small height in such a way that I might accumulate all those small intervals of time that elapse between the arrival of the heavy and light bodies respectively at their common terminus, so that this sum makes an interval of time which is not only observable, but easily observable. In order to employ the slowest speeds possible and thus reduce the change which the resisting medium produces upon the simple effect of gravity, it occurred to me to allow the bodies to fall along a plane slightly inclined to the horizontal. For in such a plane, just as well as in a vertical plane, one may discover how bodies of different weight behave: and besides this, I also wished to rid myself of the resistance which might arise from contact of the moving body with the aforesaid <term>inclined plane<note>A sloping surface used to slow down the acceleration of gravity for easier observation.</note></term>. SALV. The action of the medium in producing a greater **retardation** <term>retardation: the slowing down of an object's motion caused by external resistance</term> upon those bodies which have a less **specific gravity** <term>specific gravity: the density of a substance compared to a reference substance, like water or air</term> has already been explained by showing that they experience a **diminution of weight** <note>This refers to the effect of buoyancy; an object in a medium weighs less than it does in a vacuum because the medium pushes back against it.</note>. But to explain how one and the same 

->[132]<-

medium produces such different retardations in bodies which are made of the same material and have the same shape, but differ only in size, requires a discussion more clever than that by which one explains how a more expanded shape or an opposing motion of the medium retards the speed of the moving body. The solution of the present problem lies, I think, in the roughness and **porosity** <term>porosity: the quality of having tiny spaces or holes (pores) through which air or liquid may pass</term> which are generally and almost necessarily found in the surfaces of solid bodies. When the body is in motion these rough places strike the air or other ambient **medium** <note>The surrounding environment, such as air or water, through which the object moves.</note>. The evidence for this is found in the humming which accompanies the rapid motion of a body through air, even when that body is as round as possible. One hears not only humming, but also hissing and whistling, whenever there is any appreciable cavity or elevation upon the body. We observe also that a round solid body rotating in a lathe produces a current of air. But what more do we need? When a top spins on the ground at its greatest speed do we not hear a distinct buzzing of high pitch? This sibilant note diminishes in pitch as the speed of rotation slackens, which is evidence that these small **rugosities** <note>original: "rugosità"; the tiny bumps, wrinkles, or uneven textures on the surface of an object.</note> on the surface meet resistance in the air. There can be no doubt, therefore, that in the motion of falling bodies these rugosities strike the surrounding fluid and retard the speed; and this they do so much the more in proportion as the surface is larger, which is the case of small bodies as compared with greater.

Besides if, as you say, the larger surface suffers greater retardation the larger solid should move more slowly, which is not the fact. <meta>This page continues the "First Day" of the dialogue. Salviati is providing a geometric demonstration using cubes to show that as an object gets smaller, its surface area becomes significantly larger in proportion to its volume (and thus its weight).</meta>

# THE TWO NEW SCIENCES OF GALILEO #

Take, for example, a cube two inches on a side so that each face has an area of four square inches and the total area, i. e., the sum of the six faces, amounts to twenty-four square inches; now imagine this cube to be sawed through three times so as to divide it into eight smaller cubes, each one inch on the side, each face one inch square, and the total surface of each cube six square inches instead of twenty-four as in the case of the larger

->[134]<-

cube. It is evident therefore that the surface of the little cube is only one-fourth that of the larger, namely, the ratio of six to twenty-four; but the volume of the solid cube itself is only one-eighth; the volume, and hence also the weight, diminishes therefore much more rapidly than the surface. If we again divide the little cube into eight others we shall have, for the total surface of one of these, one and one-half square inches, which is one-sixteenth of the surface of the original cube; but its volume is only one-sixty-fourth part. Thus, by two divisions, you see that the volume is diminished four times as much as the surface. And, if the subdivision be continued until the original solid be reduced to a fine powder, we shall find that the weight of one of these smallest particles has diminished hundreds and hundreds of times as much as its surface. 

And this which I have illustrated in the case of cubes holds also in the case of all similar solids, where the volumes stand in <term>sesquialteral ratio: a mathematical relationship where the volume increases according to the 3/2 power of the surface area</term> <note>original: "proporzione sesquialtera"; this refers to the fact that for similar solids, volume scales with the cube of the length while area scales with the square.</note> to their surfaces. Observe then how much greater the resistance, arising from contact of the surface of the moving body with the medium, in the case of small bodies than in the case of large; and when one considers that the **rugosities** <term>rugosities: the microscopic roughness or textures on a surface</term> on the very small surfaces of fine dust particles are perhaps no smaller than those on the surfaces of larger solids which have been carefully polished, he will see how important it is that the medium should be very fluid and offer no resistance to being thrust aside, easily yielding to a small force. You see, therefore, Simplicio, that I was not mistaken when, not long ago, I said that the surface of a small solid is comparatively greater than that of a large one.

SIMP. I am quite convinced; and, believe me, if I were again beginning my studies, I should follow the advice of Plato and <note>Simplicio refers to the tradition that Plato's Academy had an inscription stating "Let no one ignorant of geometry enter here."</note>

This explanation does not impress me as sufficient to establish 2 and 3/2 <note>A ratio of one and a half.</note> as the natural ratios of the octave and the fifth, and my reason for thinking so is as follows. There are three different ways in which the pitch <note>Galileo uses "tone," referring to how high or low the sound is.</note> of a string may be sharpened: namely, by shortening it, by stretching it, and by making it thinner. If the tension and size of the string remain constant, one obtains the octave by shortening it to one-half—that is, by sounding first the open string and then one-half of it. But if length and size remain constant and one attempts to produce the octave by stretching, he will find that it does not suffice to double the stretching weight; it must be quadrupled. So, if the fundamental note is produced by a weight of one pound, four will be required to bring out the octave.

And finally, if the length and tension remain constant while one changes the size <margin>For the exact meaning of "size" see page 103 below. <note>Translator's note.</note></margin> of the string, he will find that in order to produce the octave, the size must be reduced to 1/4 that which gave the fundamental. And what I have said concerning the octave—namely, that its ratio as derived from the tension and size of the string is the square of that derived from the length—applies equally well to all other musical intervals <note>original: *intervalli musici*</note>.
->[144]<-
Thus, if one wishes to produce a fifth by changing the length, he finds that the ratio of the lengths must be one-and-a-half <note>original: "sesquialteral," a term for the 3:2 ratio.</note>; in other words, he sounds first the open string, then two-thirds of it. But if he wishes to produce this same result by stretching or thinning the string, then it becomes necessary to square the ratio of 3/2, which is 9/4 <note>original: *dupla sesquiquarta*, a technical term for a ratio of 2 and 1/4 (9/4).</note>. Accordingly, if the fundamental requires a weight of 4 pounds, the higher note will be produced not by 6, but by 9 pounds; the same is true in regard to size: the string which gives the fundamental is larger than that which yields the fifth in the ratio of 9 to 4.

In view of these facts, I see no reason why those wise philosophers—

**SAGR.** Such an invention would, I assure you, command my admiration.

...brass wire, we must make it, not four times as large, but four times as heavy as the **gut-string** <term>gut-string<note>Musical strings traditionally made from the processed intestines of sheep or other animals; they were the standard before the invention of modern synthetic strings.</note></term>: as regards size therefore the metal string is not four times as big but four times as heavy. The wire may therefore be even thinner than the gut notwithstanding the fact that the latter gives the higher note. Hence if two **spinets** <term>spinet<note>A small, compact keyboard instrument of the harpsichord family, popular in the 16th and 17th centuries.</note></term> are strung, one with gold wire the other with brass, and if the corresponding strings each have the same length, diameter, and tension it follows that the instrument strung with gold will have a pitch about one-fifth lower than the other because gold has a **density** <note>The mass of a substance per unit of volume. Galileo is noting that because gold is heavier than brass, it vibrates more slowly.</note> almost twice that of brass. And here it is to be noted that it is the weight rather than the size of a moving body which offers resistance to change of **speed of motion** <note>original: *velocità del moto*</note> contrary to what one might at first glance think. For it seems reasonable to believe that a body which is large and light should suffer greater retardation of motion in thrusting aside the medium than would one which is thin and heavy; yet here exactly the opposite is true.

Returning now to the original subject of discussion, I assert that the ratio of a **musical interval** <note>The distance in pitch between two sounds, which Galileo correctly identifies as a mathematical relationship.</note> is not immediately determined either by the length, size, or tension of the strings but rather by the ratio of their **frequencies** <note>The number of times a string vibrates per second.</note>, that is, by the number of pulses of air waves which strike the **tympanum** <term>tympanum<note>The eardrum; the membrane in the middle ear that vibrates in response to sound waves.</note></term> of the ear, causing it also to vibrate with the same frequency. This fact established, we may possibly explain why certain pairs of notes, differing in pitch produce a pleasing sensation, others a less pleasant effect, and still others a disagreeable sensation. Such an explanation would be tantamount to an explanation of the more or less perfect **consonances** <note>Harmonious combinations of tones that sound stable and pleasant together.</note> and of **dissonances** <note>Tones that sound clashing or "harsh" when played together.</note>. The unpleasant sensation produced by the latter arises, I think, from the discordant vibrations of two different tones which strike the ear **disproportionately** <note>original: *sproporzionatamente*; here meaning that the vibrations do not align in a simple, repeating pattern.</note>.
