...to the augmented fourth or diminished fifth <note>original: *tritono o semi-diapente*. In Galileo's time, these intervals were often called the "devil in music" because of their restless, unstable sound.</note>.

Agreeable consonances are pairs of tones which strike the ear with a certain regularity; this regularity consists in the fact that the pulses delivered by the two tones, in the same interval of time, shall be commensurable in number <note>Meaning the vibrations can be measured by simple whole-number ratios, like 2:1 or 3:2.</note>, so as not to keep the ear drum in perpetual torment, bending in two different directions in order to yield to the ever-discordant impulses.

The first and most pleasing consonance is, therefore, the octave since, for every pulse given to the **tympanum** <term>tympanum<note>The medical term for the eardrum, which vibrates when struck by sound waves.</note></term> by the lower string, the sharp string delivers two; accordingly at every other vibration of the upper string both pulses are delivered simultaneously so that one-half the entire number of pulses are delivered in unison. But when two strings are in unison their vibrations always coincide and the effect is that of a single string; hence we do not refer to it as consonance. The fifth is also a pleasing interval since for every two vibrations of the lower string the upper one gives three, so that considering the entire number of pulses from the upper string one-third of them will strike in unison, i. e., between each pair of concordant vibrations there intervene two single vibrations; and when the interval is a fourth, three single vibrations intervene. In case the interval is a second where the ratio is 9/8 it is only every ninth vibration of the upper string which reaches the ear simultaneously with one of the lower; all the others are discordant and produce a harsh effect upon the recipient ear which interprets them as dissonances.

**Technical Terms:**
*   **Vibrations:** The rapid back-and-forth movement of the string that creates sound.
*   **Unison:** When two notes are identical in pitch and their waves hit the ear at the same time.
*   **Fifth:** A musical interval where the higher note vibrates three times for every two vibrations of the lower note.
*   **Ratio 3/2:** The mathematical expression of the fifth.
*   **Pulsations/Pulse:** The individual "hits" of sound waves against the eardrum.
*   **Terminals:** The fixed endpoints of the vibrating strings.
*   **Wave length:** The physical distance a sound vibration travels.

**SAGREDO.** While Simplicio and I were awaiting your arrival we were trying to recall that last consideration which you advanced as a principle and basis for the results you intended to obtain; this consideration dealt with the resistance which all solids offer to fracture and depended upon a certain <term>cement</term> <note>The internal binding force or "glue" holding the particles of a solid body together.</note> which held the parts glued together so that they would yield and separate only under a powerful pull <note>original: "potente attrazzione"</note>. ## PROPOSITION I

A prism or solid cylinder of glass, steel, wood or other breakable material which is capable of sustaining a very heavy weight when applied longitudinally <note>original: "per lo lungo"; meaning a "stretching" or tensile force pulling from the end.</note> is, as previously remarked, easily broken by the transverse <note>original: "per traverso"; meaning a force applied at a right angle to the length, like a weight hanging from a beam.</note> application of a weight which may be much smaller in proportion as the length of the cylinder exceeds its thickness.

<margin>The ratio of length CB to half the thickness BA equals the ratio of the Weight to the Resistance.</margin>

Let us imagine a solid prism ABCD fastened into a wall at the end AB, and supporting a weight E at the other end; understand also that the wall is vertical and that the prism or cylinder is fastened at right angles to the wall. It is clear that, if the cylinder breaks, fracture will occur at the point B where the edge of the mortise <note>The hole or slot in the wall where the beam is fixed.</note> acts as a fulcrum for the lever BC, to which the force is applied; the thickness of the solid BA is the other arm of the lever along which is located the resistance. This resistance opposes the separation of the part BD, lying outside the wall, from that portion lying inside. From the preceding, it follows that the <term>moment<note>For Galileo, "moment" (momento) refers to the total "power" or "efficacy" of a weight, which increases with its distance from the fulcrum.</note></term> of the force applied at C bears to the <term>moment</term> of the resistance, found in the thickness of the prism, i. e., in the attachment of the base BA to its contiguous parts, the same ratio which the length CB bears to half the length BA.

If now we define **absolute resistance** to fracture <insert>[157]</insert> as that offered to a longitudinal pull (in which case the stretching force acts in the same direction as that through which the body is moved), then it follows that the absolute resistance of the prism BD is to the breaking load placed at the end of the lever BC in the same ratio as the length BC is to the half of AB in the case of a prism, or the semidiameter in the case of a cylinder. This is our first proposition.

### PROPOSITION III

Considering now the case of a <term>prism</term> <note>A solid geometric figure with two identical ends and flat sides; Galileo uses this to refer to rectangular beams.</note> or cylinder growing longer in a horizontal direction, we must find out in what ratio the <term>moment</term> <note>In modern physics, this is known as "torque" or the turning effect of a force.</note> of its own weight increases in comparison with its resistance to fracture. This moment I find increases in propor-<insert>[159]</insert>tion to the square of the length. In order to prove this let AD be a prism or cylinder lying horizontal with its end A firmly fixed in a wall. Let the length of the prism be increased by the addition of the portion BE. It is clear that merely changing the length of the lever from AB to AC will, if we disregard its weight, increase the moment of the force <insert>[at the end]</insert> tending to produce fracture at A in the ratio of CA to BA. But, besides this, the weight of the solid portion BE, added to the weight of the solid AB increases the moment of the total weight in the ratio of the weight of the prism AE to that of the prism AB, which is the same as the ratio of the length AC to AB.

It follows, therefore, that, when the length and weight are simultaneously increased in any given proportion, the moment, which is the product of these two, is increased in a ratio which is the square of the preceding proportion. The conclusion is then that the bending moments due to the weight of prisms and cylinders which have the same thickness but different lengths,

### PROPOSITION V

Prisms and cylinders which differ in both length and thickness offer <term>resistances to fracture</term> <note>Galileo is referring to what we now call "flexural strength" or the ability of a beam to resist breaking when loaded from the side.</note> which are directly proportional to the cubes of the diameters of their bases and inversely proportional to their lengths.

->[163]<-

Let ABC and DEF be two such cylinders; then the resistance of the cylinder AC bears to the resistance of the cylinder DF a ratio which is the product of the cube of the diameter AB divided by the cube of the diameter DE, and of the length EF divided by the length BC. Make EG equal to BC: let H be a <term>third proportional</term> <note>A geometric method for expressing squares: if A:B = B:C, then C is the third proportional. Here, it is used to build up to a cubic relationship.</note> to the lines AB and DE; let I be a fourth proportional, [so that the ratio of AB to DE is the same as H to I]: and let the ratio of I to S be the same as the ratio of length EF to BC.

<image-desc>Figure 22: A technical diagram showing two cylinders and a set of line segments. The top cylinder (AC) is shorter and thicker. Now, since the resistance of the cylinder AC is to that of the cylinder DG as the cube of AB is to the cube of DE (which is the same as the ratio of the length AB to the length I); and since the resistance of the cylinder DG is to that of the cylinder DF as the length FE is to EG (which is the same as the ratio of I to S), it follows that the ratio of the length AB to S is the same as the ratio of the resistance of cylinder AC to that of cylinder DF. But the line AB bears to S a ratio which is the product of AB/I and I/S. Hence the resistance of the cylinder AC bears to the resistance of the cylinder DF a ratio which is the product of the cube of the diameters (AB³/DE³) and of the lengths (EF/BC): which is what I intended to prove.

### PROPOSITION VI

### PROPOSITION VII

Among heavy prisms and cylinders of similar figure, there is one and only one which under the stress of its own weight lies just on the limit between breaking and not breaking: so that every larger one is unable to carry the load of its own weight and breaks; while every smaller one is able to withstand some additional force tending to break it.

Let AB be a heavy prism, the longest possible that will just sustain its own weight, so that if it be lengthened the least bit it will break. will break under its own weight, and every smaller one will not break, but will be able to withstand some force in addition to its own weight.

Now since the resistance <gloss>bending strength</gloss> of the base DC is to the resistance of the base KL as the square of DC is to the square of KL, that is, as the square of KL is to the square of MN, or, as the cylinder E is to the cylinder X, that is, as the moment <term>moment</term> <note>The "moment" refers to the stress or turning force exerted by the weight of the cylinder itself at the point where it is supported.</note> E is to the moment X; and since also the resistance [bending strength] of the base KL is to the resistance of the base MN as the cube of KL is to the cube of MN, that is, as the cube of DC is to the cube of KL, or, as the cylinder A is to the cylinder E, that is, as the moment of A is to the moment of E; hence it follows, *by equality in perturbed proportion*, <note>original: "ex æquali in proportione perturbata." This is a technical term from Euclidean geometry (Book V, Definition 20) describing a specific way of comparing ratios across two sets of magnitudes when the ratios are ordered differently.</note> that the moment of A is to the moment of X as the resistance of the base DC is to the resistance of the base MN; therefore moment and resistance are related to each other in prism X precisely as they are in prism A.

From what has already been demonstrated, you can plainly see the impossibility of increasing the size of structures to vast dimensions either in art or in nature; likewise the impossibility of building ships, palaces, or temples of enormous size in such a way that their oars, yards, beams, iron-bolts, and, in short, all their other parts will hold together; nor can nature produce trees of extraordinary size because the branches would break down under their own weight; so also it would be impossible to build up the bony structures of men, horses, or other animals so as to hold together and perform their normal functions if these animals were to be increased enormously in height; for this increase in height can be accomplished only by employing a material which is harder and stronger than usual, or by enlarging the size of the bones, thus changing their shape until the form and appearance of the animals suggest a monstrosity. Whereas, if the size of a body be diminished, the strength of that body is not diminished in the same proportion; indeed the smaller the body the greater its relative strength. Thus a small dog could probably carry on his back two or three dogs of his own size; but I believe that a horse could not carry even one of his own size.

one which had hitherto escaped my attention and which enables giants and other animals of vast size to support themselves and to move about as well as smaller animals do. ### SECOND DAY

Hence, if the bones are heavier, it is necessary that the muscles or other constituents of the body should be lighter in order that their **buoyancy** <note>Buoyancy here refers to the upward force exerted by a fluid that opposes the weight of an immersed object.</note> may counterbalance the weight of the bones. In aquatic animals, therefore, circumstances are just reversed from what they are with land animals. In land animals, the bones must sustain not only their own weight but also that of the flesh; however, in aquatic animals, it is the flesh which supports not only its own weight but also that of the bones. We must therefore cease to wonder why these enormously large animals inhabit the water rather than the land—that is to say, the air.

**SIMPLICIO:** I am convinced, and I only wish to add that what we call land animals ought really to be called "air animals," seeing that they live in the air, are surrounded by air, and breathe air.

**SAGREDO:** I have enjoyed Simplicio’s discussion, including both the question raised and its answer. Another rather interesting problem may be solved as a consequence of this theorem, namely:

> **Given the maximum weight which a cylinder or prism can support at its middle-point (where the resistance is a minimum), and given also a larger weight, find that point in the cylinder for which this larger weight is the maximum load that can be supported.**

Let that one of the given weights which is larger than the maximum weight supported at the middle of the cylinder **AB** bear to this maximum weight the same ratio which the length **E** bears to the length **F**. The problem is to find that point in the cylinder at which this larger weight becomes the maximum that can be supported. 

Let **G** be a **mean proportional** <term>mean proportional: A value that relates to two others such that the first is to the mean as the mean is to the second (E:G = G:F). In modern algebra, this is equivalent to G² = E × F.</term> between the lengths **E** and **F**. Draw **AD** and **S** so that they bear to each other the same ratio as **E** to **G**; accordingly, **S** will be less than **AD**.

Let **AD** be the **diameter** of a **semicircle AHD**, in which take **AH** equal to **S**; join the points **H** and **D** and lay off **DR** equal to **HD**. Then, I say, **R** is the point sought—namely, the point at which the given weight (which is greater than the maximum supported at the middle of the cylinder **D**) would become the maximum load.

On **AB** as diameter draw the semicircle **ANB**: erect the **perpendicular** <note>A line standing at a right angle (90 degrees) to the base line.</note> **RN** and join the points **N** and **D**. Now since the sum of the squares on **NR** and **RD** is equal to the square of **ND** (that is, the square of **AD**, or to the sum of the squares of **AH** and **HD**); and, since the square of **HD** is equal to the square of **DR**, it follows that the square of **NR** (that is, the rectangle **AR.RB**) is equal to the square of **AH**, also therefore to the square of **S**; but the square of **S** is to the square of **AD** as the length **F** is to the length **E**, that is, as the maximum weight...

# THIRD DAY

## CHANGE OF POSITION <note>original: *De Motu Locali* — literally "Concerning Local Motion," the study of how objects move through space.</note>

<image-desc>Ornamental woodcut initial 'M' showing a cherub or putto leaning against a shield-shaped frame containing the letter.</image-desc>
My purpose is to set forth a very new science dealing with a very ancient subject. There is, in nature, perhaps nothing older than **motion**, concerning which the books written by philosophers are neither few nor small; <margin>On Local Motion</margin> nevertheless I have discovered by experiment some properties of it which are worth knowing and which have not hitherto been either observed or demonstrated. Some superficial observations have been made, as, for instance, that the **natural motion** <note>original: *naturalem motum*</note> of a heavy falling body is continuously accelerated;* but to just what extent this acceleration occurs has not yet been announced; for so far as I know, no one has yet pointed out that the distances traversed, during equal intervals of time, by a body falling from rest, stand to one another in the same ratio as the **odd numbers** beginning with unity <note>meaning the number one</note>.†

It has been observed that missiles and projectiles describe a curved path of some sort; however no one has pointed out the fact that this path is a **parabola**. But this and other facts, not few in number or less worth knowing, I have succeeded in proving; and what I consider more important, there have been opened up to this vast and most excellent science, of which my—

† A theorem demonstrated on page 175 below. <insert>[Translator's Note]</insert>

work is merely the beginning, ways and means by which other minds more acute than mine will explore its remote corners. 

This discussion is divided into three parts: 
1. The first part deals with motion which is **steady** or **uniform**; 
2. The second treats of motion as we find it **accelerated** in nature; 
3. The third deals with the so-called **violent motions** <note>In the physics of Galileo’s time, "violent motion" referred to movement caused by an external force, like a catapult or a throw, as opposed to "natural motion" like a stone falling due to gravity.</note> and with **projectiles**.

### UNIFORM MOTION

In dealing with steady or uniform motion, we need a single definition which I give as follows:

### DEFINITION

By **steady** or **uniform motion**, I mean one in which the distances covered by the moving particle during **any** equal intervals of time, are themselves equal.

### CAUTION

We must add to the old definition (which defined steady motion simply as one in which equal distances are covered in equal times) the word “**any**,” meaning by this, *all* equal intervals of time. 

For it may happen that a moving body traverses equal distances during some specific equal intervals of time, and yet the distances covered during smaller portions of those time-intervals might not be equal. <note>Galileo is being mathematically precise here: to be truly uniform, the speed must not fluctuate even for a moment. If a car travels 60 miles in one hour and another 60 miles in the next, it might seem uniform; however, if it sped up and slowed down within those hours, it is not "uniform motion" by his definition.</note>

From the above definition, four **axioms** <note>In science and math, an axiom is a self-evident rule that serves as a starting point for further reasoning.</note> follow, namely:

### AXIOM I

In the case of one and the same uniform motion, the distance covered during a longer interval of time is greater than the distance covered during a shorter interval of time.

### AXIOM II

In the case of one and the same uniform motion, the time required to cover a greater distance is longer than the time required for a shorter distance.

<summary>Galileo establishes the mathematical foundation for uniform motion, providing a rigorous definition that requires consistency across every possible interval of time. This precision allowed him to move beyond vague philosophical descriptions of movement into modern kinematics.</summary>

### AXIOM III

In one and the same interval of time, the distance traversed at a greater speed is larger than the distance traversed at a less speed. <note>Essentially, if two objects move for the same amount of time, the faster one goes further.</note>

[192]
### AXIOM IV

The speed required to traverse a longer distance is greater than that required to traverse a shorter distance during the same time-interval. <note>This is the logical converse of Axiom III: to cover more ground in the same time, you must move faster.</note>

### THEOREM I, PROPOSITION I

If a moving particle, carried uniformly at a constant speed, traverses two distances, the time-intervals required are to each other in the ratio of these distances. <note>In modern terms: if speed is constant, time is directly proportional to distance. For example, if you travel twice as far, it will take exactly twice as long.</note>

If GB is greater than BH, then IE will also be greater than EK; and if it is less, it will be less. [193] <note>This number refers to the pagination of the standard 17th-century Latin/Italian edition, used by scholars to coordinate different translations.</note>

But it has been proved that *both* of these latter quantities (the multiples IE and GB) are either equal to, greater than, or less than the time EK and the space BH, which are themselves arbitrary multiples of the second and the fourth quantities. Therefore, the first is to the second (the distance AB is to the distance BC) as the third is to the fourth (the time DE is to the time EF). **Which was to be demonstrated.** <note>original: "Q. E. ### NATURALLY ACCELERATED MOTION
<note>Original Latin title: DE MOTU NATURALITER ACCELERATO.</note>

The properties belonging to <term>uniform motion: movement at a constant speed where the distance covered is directly proportional to the time elapsed</term> have been dis-
cussed in the preceding section; but <term>accelerated motion: motion that increases in speed as it progresses</term> remains
to be considered.

And first of all it seems desirable to find and explain a defini-
tion best fitting natural phenomena. For anyone may invent an
arbitrary type of motion and discuss its properties; thus, for
instance, some have imagined <term>helices: spiral-shaped curves</term> and <term>conchoids: a specific type of shell-like curve studied by ancient mathematicians</term> as described
by certain motions which are not met with in nature, and have
very commendably established the properties which these curves
possess in virtue of their definitions; but we have decided to con-
sider the phenomena of bodies falling with an acceleration such
as actually occurs in nature and to make this definition of
<term>accelerated motion</term> exhibit the essential features of observed
accelerated motions. And this, at last, after repeated efforts we
trust we have succeeded in doing. In this belief we are confirmed
mainly by the consideration that experimental results are seen
to agree with and exactly correspond with those properties
which have been, one after another, demonstrated by us.
Finally, in the investigation of <term>naturally accelerated motion</term> we
were led, by hand as it were, in following the habit and custom of
nature herself...

nature herself, in all her various other processes, to employ only those means which are most common, simple and easy. <note>Galileo relies on the philosophical principle of parsimony—the idea that nature always chooses the simplest path—to justify his mathematical model of how objects fall.</note>

For I think no one believes that swimming or flying can be accomplished in a manner simpler or easier than that instinctively employed by fishes and birds.

When, therefore, I observe a stone initially at rest falling from an elevated position and continually acquiring new increments of speed, why should I not believe that such increases take place in a manner which is exceedingly simple and rather obvious to everybody? If now we examine the matter carefully we find no addition or increment more simple than that which repeats itself always in the same manner. This we readily understand when we consider the intimate relationship between time and motion; for just as <term>uniformity of motion: movement at a constant speed where the distance covered is exactly proportional to the time passed</term> is defined by and conceived through equal times and equal spaces (thus we call a motion uniform when equal distances are traversed during equal time-intervals), so also we may, in a similar manner, through equal time-intervals, conceive additions of speed as taking place without complication; thus we may picture to our
<insert>[198]</insert>
mind a motion as <term>uniformly and continuously accelerated: motion where the velocity increases by equal amounts in every equal interval of time</term> when, during any equal intervals of time whatever, equal increments of speed are given to it. <note>This is a revolutionary moment in science: defining acceleration as a function of time. Before Galileo, many scientists tried to define acceleration by how much speed was gained over a certain distance, which leads to much more complex mathematics.</note> Thus if any equal intervals of time whatever have elapsed, counting from the time at which the moving body left its position of rest and began to descend, the amount of speed acquired during the first two time-intervals will be double that acquired during the first time-interval alone; so the amount added during three of these time-intervals will be treble; and that in four, quadruple that of the first time-interval. To put the matter more clearly, if a body were to continue its motion with the same speed which it had acquired during the first time-interval and were to retain this same uniform speed, then its motion would be twice as slow as that which it would have if its velocity had been acquired during *two* time-intervals.

And thus, it seems, we shall not be far wrong if we put the increment of speed as proportional to the increment of time;

### THEOREM I, PROPOSITION I

The time in which any space is traversed by a body starting from rest and **uniformly accelerated** is equal to the time in which that same space would be traversed by the same body moving at a **uniform speed** whose value is the mean of the highest speed and the speed just before acceleration began.

<image-desc>
A geometric diagram labeled "Fig. 47". On the far right is a vertical line segment with points C at the top and D at the bottom, representing the distance traveled. To the left is a geometric figure representing velocity over time. A vertical line AB serves as the time axis. A horizontal line EB represents the maximum speed reached at the end of the time interval. A diagonal line AE forms a triangle AEB, representing the uniformly increasing speed. Superimposed on this is a rectangle AGFB, where F is the midpoint of EB and G is a point such that GA is parallel to FB. This rectangle represents motion at a constant mean speed. Horizontal parallel lines are drawn within the shapes to represent speeds at specific instants. A point I is marked where the diagonal AE intersects the vertical line GF.
</image-desc>

Let us represent by the line AB the time in which the space CD is traversed by a body which starts from rest at C and is uniformly accelerated; let the final and highest value of the speed gained during the interval AB be represented by the line EB drawn at right angles to AB; draw the line AE, then all lines drawn from equidistant points on AB and parallel to BE will represent the increasing values of the speed, beginning with the instant A. 

Let the point F bisect the line EB; draw FG parallel to BA, and GA parallel to FB, thus forming a parallelogram AGFB which will be equal in area to the triangle AEB, since the side GF bisects the side AE at the point I; for if the parallel lines in the triangle AEB are extended to GI, then the sum of all the parallels contained in the quadrilateral is equal to the sum of those contained in the triangle AEB; for those in the triangle IEF are equal to those contained in the triangle GIA, while those included in the <term>trapezium <note>A four-sided shape with at least one pair of parallel sides; here used to describe the shared area AIFB.</note></term> AIFB are common. 

Since each and every instant of time in the time-interval AB has its corresponding point on the line AB, from which points parallels drawn in and limited by the triangle AEB represent the increasing values of the growing velocity, and since parallels contained within the rectangle represent the values of a speed which is not increasing, but constant; it appears, in like manner, that the <term>momenta <note>original: *momenta*; in this context, Galileo refers to the "impetus" or the instantaneous quantity of motion an object possesses at any given moment.</note></term> assumed by the moving body may also be represented, in the case of the accelerated motion, by the increasing parallels of the triangle AEB, while in the case of uniform motion they are represented by the parallels of the rectangle AGFB. For what the moments of speed lack in the first part of the accelerated motion (the moments represented by the parallels in the triangle GIA being missing) is made up by the moments represented by the parallels of the triangle IEF.

It follows, therefore, that equal spaces will be traversed in the same time by two bodies, one of which starts from rest and moves with uniform acceleration, while the other moves with a uniform speed which is one-half the maximum speed of the first. **Q.E.D.** <note>original: *Quod Erat Demonstrandum*; a Latin phrase meaning "which was to be demonstrated," traditionally used at the end of a mathematical proof.</note>

### THEOREM II, PROPOSITION II

**The spaces described by a body falling from rest with a uniformly accelerated motion are to each other as the squares of the time-intervals employed in traversing these distances.**

Let the time beginning with any instant A be represented by the straight line AB in which are taken any two time-intervals AD and AE. Let HI represent the distance through which the body, starting from rest at H, falls with uniform acceleration. If HL represents the space traversed during the time-interval AD, and HM that covered during the interval AE, then the space MH stands to the space LH in a ratio which is the square of the ratio of the time AE to the time AD; or we may say simply that the distances HM and HL are related as the squares of AE and AD.

Draw the line AC making any angle whatever with the line AB; and from the points D and E, draw the parallel lines DO and EP; of these two lines, DO represents the greatest velocity attained during the interval AD, while EP represents the maximum velocity acquired during the interval AE. ## COROLLARY I

Hence it is clear that if we take any equal intervals of time whatever, counting from the beginning of the motion, such as AD, DE, EF, FG, in which the spaces HL, LM, MN, NI are traversed, these spaces will bear to one another the same ratio as the series of odd numbers, 1, 3, 5, 7; for this is the ratio of the differences of the squares of the lines [which represent time], differences which exceed one another by equal amounts, this excess being equal to the smallest line [namely the one representing a single time-interval]: or we may say [that this is the ratio] of the differences of the squares of the natural numbers beginning with unity. <note>Galileo is observing a beautiful mathematical pattern: if a ball falls 1 unit of distance in the first second, it will fall 3 units in the next, 5 in the third, and so on. ### THIRD DAY

The time interval CI will be increased by an amount represented by the parallel lines within the triangle BFG, which is equal in area to the triangle ABC. If one then adds to the velocity GI <note>The speed reached at the end of the second time interval.</note> half of the velocity FG—which is the highest speed acquired through <term>accelerated motion</term> <note>Motion that constantly increases in speed over time.</note> as shown by the lines in triangle BFG—he will find the <term>uniform velocity</term> <note>A steady, unchanging speed.</note> required to cover that same distance in the time CI. Since this resulting speed IN is three times as great as the speed EC, it follows that the distance covered during the interval CI is three times as great as the distance covered during the first interval AC.

Let us imagine the motion extended over another equal time-interval IO, and the triangle extended to APO. It is then evident that if the motion continues during the interval IO at the constant rate IF—the speed acquired by acceleration during the total time AI—the space traversed during this new interval IO will be four times that traversed during the first interval AC; this is because the speed IF is four times the speed EC. 

But if we enlarge our triangle to include the area FPQ, which is equal to the original triangle ABC, and still assume the acceleration to be constant, we must add an increment RQ (equal to the original speed EC) to the uniform speed. Then, the value of the equivalent uniform speed during the time-interval IO will be five times that of the first interval AC. Therefore, the distance traversed will be five times (quintuple) that of the first interval AC. 

It is thus evident by simple calculation that a moving body starting from rest and acquiring velocity at a rate proportional to the time, will, during equal intervals of time, traverse distances which are related to each other as the **odd numbers** beginning with **unity**—1, 3, 5; * or, considering the total space traversed, that covered

-><margin>212</margin><note>This mark indicates the page number in the original 1638 Italian edition.</note><-

in double the time will be four times (quadruple) that covered during a single unit of time; in triple the time, the space is nine times as great as in the first unit of time.

->*s* = 1/2 *g* (*t*₂² - *t*₁²) = *g*/2 (*t*₂ + *t*₁) (*t*₂ - *t*₁)<- 
In this formula, *g* represents the <term>acceleration of gravity</term> <note>The constant rate at which the Earth pulls objects downward.</note> and *s* is the distance covered between two moments in time, *t*₁ and *t*₂. We also observed that the times of descent, for various inclinations of the plane, bore to one another precisely that ratio which, as we shall see later, the Author <note>The "Author" refers to Galileo himself.</note> had predicted and demonstrated for them.

For the measurement of time, we employed a large vessel of water placed in an elevated position; to the bottom of this vessel was soldered a pipe of small diameter giving a thin jet of water, which we collected in a small glass during the time of each descent, whether for the whole length of the channel or for a part of its length; the water thus collected was weighed, after each descent, on a very accurate balance; the differences and ratios of these weights gave us the differences and ratios of the times, and this with such accuracy that although the operation was repeated many, many times, there was no appreciable discrepancy in the results.

**SIMPLICIO:** I would like to have been present at these experiments; but feeling confidence in the care with which you performed them, and in the fidelity with which you relate them, I am satisfied and accept them as true and valid.

**SALVIATI:** Then we can proceed without discussion.

## COROLLARY II

Secondly, it follows that, starting from any initial point, if we take any two distances traversed in any time-intervals whatsoever, these time-intervals bear to one another the same ratio as one of the distances to the **mean proportional** <note>In geometry, a mean proportional (or geometric mean) between two values is the square root of their product. If you have distances A and B, the mean proportional is C where A/C = C/B.</note> of the two distances.

<margin><image-desc>A vertical diagram consisting of a line with four points labeled from top to bottom: S, T, X, and Y. Point X is marked with a horizontal cross-bar. To the left of the diagram is the text "Fig. 50".</image-desc> Fig. 50</margin> For if we take two distances ST and SY measured from the initial point S, the mean proportional of which is SX, the time of fall through ST is to the time of fall through SY as ST is to SX; or one may say the time of fall through SY is to the time of fall through ST as SY is to SX. Now since it has been shown that the spaces traversed are in the same ratio as the squares of the times; and since, moreover, the ratio of the space SY to the space ST is the square of the ratio SY to SX, it follows that the ratio of the times of fall through SY and ST is the ratio of the respective distances SY and SX.

## SCHOLIUM <note>A scholium is a marginal note or explanatory commentary in an ancient or medieval manuscript.</note>

The above corollary has been proven for the case of vertical fall; but it holds also for planes inclined at any angle; for it is to be assumed that along these planes the velocity increases in the same ratio, that is, in proportion to the time, or, if you prefer, as the series of natural numbers.*

SALV. <note>Salviati is the character in the dialogue who represents Galileo’s own views.</note> Here, Sagredo, I should like, if it be not too tedious to Simplicio, to interrupt for a moment the present discussion in order to make some additions on the basis of what has already been proved and of what mechanical principles we have already learned from our Academician <note>The "Academician" is Galileo himself, referred to as the author of the work being discussed.</note>. This addition I make for the better establishment on logical and experimental grounds, of the principle which we have above considered; and what is more important, for the purpose of deriving it geometrically, after first demonstrating a single **lemma** <note>A "lemma" is a secondary or intermediate theorem used as a stepping stone to prove a larger point.</note> which is fundamental in the science of motion [<term>impeti</term> <note>original: "impeti". In Galileo’s time, this referred to "impetus," the power or force possessed by a moving body, which we now associate with momentum or kinetic energy.</note>].

### THIRD DAY

**SAGREDO.** If the advance which you propose to make is such as will confirm and fully establish these sciences of motion, I will gladly devote to it any length of time. Indeed, I shall not only
->[215]<-
be glad to have you proceed, but I beg of you at once to satisfy the curiosity which you have awakened in me concerning your proposition; and I think that **Simplicio** is of the same mind.

**SIMPLICIO.** Quite right.

**SALVIATI.** Since then I have your permission, let us first of all consider this notable fact, that the momenta or speeds <note>original: "i momenti o le velocità." In Galileo's time, "momento" (momentum) often referred to the "effective weight" or the force driving an object down a slope, rather than the modern definition of mass times velocity.</note> of one and the same moving body vary with the inclination of the plane. 

The speed reaches a maximum along a vertical direction, and for other directions diminishes as the plane diverges from the vertical. Therefore the impetus, natural inclination, energy <note>original: "l'impeto, il talento, l'energia." The word "talento" here refers to a natural propensity or "talent" for a body to move toward its center.</note>, or, one might say, the momentum <note>original: "il momento"</note> of descent of the moving body is diminished by the plane upon which it is supported and along which it rolls. 

For the sake of greater clearness erect the line AB perpendicular to the horizontal AC; next draw AD, AE, AF, etc., at different inclinations to the horizontal. Then I say that all the momentum of the falling body is along the vertical and is a maximum when it falls in that direction; the momentum is less along DA and still less along EA, and even less yet along the more inclined plane FA.

Finally on the horizontal plane the momentum vanishes altogether; the body finds itself in a condition of indifference as to motion or rest; has no inherent tendency to move in any direction, and offers no resistance to being set in motion. For just as a heavy body or system of bodies cannot of itself move upwards, or recede from the common center <note>original: "comun centro." This refers to the center of the Earth, which in the Aristotelian and early Galilean worldview was the point toward which all "heavy" things naturally tended to fall.</note> toward which all heavy things tend, so it is impossible for any body of its own accord to assume any motion other than one which carries it nearer to the aforesaid common center.

A horizontal line AC extends to the left from A. Several lines (AD, AE, AF) are drawn from point A at different angles reaching toward the left and up. A small circle (a ball) is placed at point G on the line AF. A dashed vertical line drops from point F to point H on the horizontal line AC.</image-desc>

Hence, along the horizontal, by which we understand a surface, every point of which is equidistant from this same common center, the body will have no momentum whatever.

Since the change of momentum <note>original: "momento." He included it in a treatise on mechanics prepared solely for the use of his students, proving it thoroughly when considering the origin and nature of that marvelous machine, the screw. What he demonstrated is the way in which the momentum <note>original: "impeto"</note> varies according to the slope of the plane—for instance, the plane FA, where one end is raised by a vertical distance FC. This vertical direction FC is the path along which the momentum of a heavy body reaches its maximum. Let us discover what ratio this maximum momentum bears to the momentum of the same body moving along the inclined plane FA. This ratio, I say, is the inverse of the ratio of those lengths <note>Meaning the force required to hold a weight on an incline is to the weight of the body as the height of the incline is to its length.</note>. This is the lemma <note>A preliminary proposition used to prove a subsequent theorem.</note> preceding the theorem which I hope to demonstrate a little later.

It is clear that the impelling force <note>original: "impeto"</note> acting on a body during its descent is equal to the resistance or minimum force <note>original: "resistenza o forza minima"</note> sufficient to hold it at rest. To measure this force and resistance <note>original: "forza e resistenza"</note>, I propose to use the weight of another body. Let us place a body G upon the plane FA and connect it to a weight H by means of a cord passing over the point F. In this setup, the body H will ascend or descend along the perpendicular line for the same distance that the body G ascends or descends along the inclined plane FA. However, this distance will not be equal to the vertical rise or fall of G—and it is in the vertical direction alone that G, like all other heavy bodies, exerts its resistance <note>original: "resistenza"</note>. This is clear. For if we consider the motion of the body G from A to F within the triangle AFC, we see it is made up of a horizontal component AC and a vertical component CF. We must remember that this body experiences no resistance to motion along the horizontal, because by such a
[217]
motion the body neither gains nor loses distance from the common center of heavy things <note>original: "centro de' gravi," referring to the center of gravity or the center of the Earth.</note>. Since the body G, in moving from A to F, offers resistance only insofar as it rises through the vertical distance CF, while the other body H must fall vertically through the entire distance FA—and since this ratio is maintained whether the motion be large or small, the two bodies being connected by a cord that cannot stretch—we are able to assert positively that, in the case of equilibrium (where the bodies are at rest), the

# THIRD DAY

The momenta, the velocities, or their tendency to motion <note>original: "propensioni al moto." Galileo is describing the internal "urge" or physical inclination of an object to begin moving.</note>—that is, the distances they would cover in equal amounts of time—must be in inverse proportion to their weights. This is what has been demonstrated in every case of mechanical motion. <note>The original translator notes that this is a near approach to the "principle of virtual work" formally stated by John Bernoulli in 1717, which relates the work done by forces to the displacement of the system.</note> Therefore, to keep weight G at rest, one must provide a weight H that is smaller in the same ratio as the distance CF is smaller than FA. If we do this, the ratio of FA to FC will equal the ratio of weight G to weight H; then equilibrium <term>Equilibrium: A state of balance where opposing forces cancel each other out, resulting in no movement.</term> will occur. That is, the weights H and G will have equal impelling forces <note>original: "momenti eguali"</note>, and the two bodies will come to rest.

Since we are agreed that the impetus, energy, momentum, or tendency to motion of a moving body is equal to the force or minimum resistance <note>original: "forza o resistenza minima"</note> sufficient to stop it, and since we have found that weight H is capable of preventing motion in weight G, it follows that the smaller weight H—whose entire force <note>original: "momento totale"</note> acts along the perpendicular vertical line FC—will be an exact measure of the partial force <note>original: "momento parziale"</note> that the larger weight G exerts along the sloped plane FA. 

But the measure of the total force <note>original: "total momento"</note> on the body G is its own weight, since to prevent its fall it is only necessary to balance it with an equal weight (provided this second weight is free to move vertically); therefore, the partial force of G along the inclined plane FA will bear the same ratio to the maximum and total force of G along the vertical FC as the weight H bears to the weight G. This ratio is, by construction, the same ratio that the height, FC, of the inclined plane bears to its length FA. We have here the lemma <note>A preliminary proposition used as a stepping stone to prove a larger theorem.</note> which I proposed to demonstrate and which, as you will see, has been assumed by our Author <note>Galileo's way of referring to himself throughout the dialogue.</note> in the second part of the sixth proposition of this treatise.

**SAGREDO:** From what you have shown thus far, it appears to me that one might infer—arguing from equal ratios through perturbed proportion <note>original: "ex aequali con la proportione perturbata." A technical term from Euclidean geometry used when comparing two sets of ratios to find a third relationship.</note>—that the tendencies <note>original: "momenti"</note> of one and the same body to move along planes with different inclinations, but sharing the same vertical height (such as FA and FI), are to each other inversely as the lengths of those planes.

### Theorem: Equal Speeds from Equal Heights

**If a body falls freely along smooth planes inclined at any angle whatsoever, but of the same height, the speeds with which it reaches the bottom are the same.**

First we must recall the fact that on a plane of any inclination whatever a body starting from rest gains speed or momentum <note>original: "la quantità dell’ impeto." In Galileo's time, "impetus" was a precursor to our modern concept of momentum—the "quantity" of motion an object possesses.</note> in direct proportion to the time, in agreement with the definition of naturally accelerated motion <term>Naturally accelerated motion: A motion where the speed increases by equal amounts in equal intervals of time, such as an object in free fall.</term> given by the Author. Hence, as he has shown in the preceding proposition, the distances traversed are proportional to the squares of the times and therefore to the squares of the speeds. The speed relations are here the same as in the motion first studied [i. e., vertical motion], since in each case the gain of speed is proportional to the time.

Let AB be an inclined plane whose height above the level BC is AC. As we have seen above the force impelling <note>original: "l’ impeto"</note> a body

A dashed line connects vertex A to point E.</image-desc>

to fall along the vertical AC is to the force which drives the same body along the inclined plane AB as AB is to AC. On the incline AB, lay off AD a third proportional <term>Third proportional: A geometric relationship where the ratio of the first length to the second is the same as the second to the third (AB : AC = AC : AD).</term> to AB and AC; then the force producing motion along AC is to that along AB (i. e., along AD) as the length AC is to the length AD. And therefore the body will traverse the space AD, along the incline AB, in the same time which it would occupy in falling the vertical distance AC, (since the forces <note>original: "momenti"</note> are in the same ratio as these distances); also the speed at C is to the speed at D as the distance AC is to the distance AD. 

But, according to the definition of accelerated motion, the speed at B is to the speed of the same body at D as the time required to traverse AB is to the time required for AD; and, according to the last corollary of the second proposition, the time of passing through the distance AB bears to the time of passing through AD the same ratio as the distance AC (a mean proportional between AB and AD) to AD. Accordingly the two speeds at B and C each bear to the speed at D the same ratio, namely, that of the distances AC and AD; hence they are equal. This is the theorem which I set out to prove.

From the above we are better able to demonstrate the following third proposition of the Author in which he employs the following principle, namely, the time required to traverse an inclined plane

For, according to the second corollary of the second proposition, if BA represents the time required to pass over the distance BA, the time required to pass over the distance AD will be a mean proportional <term>mean proportional: A middle value in a geometric sequence (like 'b' in a:b = b:c). In like manner it can be shown that the time required to fall through AC is to the time required for any other incline AE as the length AC is to the length AE; therefore, from equality <note>original: "ex aequali." ### THEOREM IV, PROPOSITION IV

let BE represent the height of the plane AB, and BD the height of BC; also let BI be a mean proportional <note>A geometric mean: a value that sits between two others in a specific mathematical proportion.</note> to BD and BE; then the ratio of BD to BI is equal to the square root of the ratio of BD to BE. <image-desc>A geometric diagram labeled Fig. 54. It depicts a vertical line segment BD meeting a horizontal line CD at a right angle at D. A line segment BC forms an inclined plane. <term>descent</term>: the motion of an object moving downward under the influence of gravity.
<term>inclined planes</term>: sloping surfaces used in physics experiments to "dilute" gravity, making the speed of falling objects easier to measure.
<term>ratio</term>: the relationship between two amounts showing the number of times one value contains or is contained within the other.
<term>mean proportional</term>: the middle term in a geometric progression (e.g., in 4:6 = 6:9, the number 6 is the mean proportional).
<term>inverse ratio</term>: a relationship where one value increases as another decreases.
<term>square roots</term>: a factor of a number that, when multiplied by itself, gives the original number; used here to describe the geometric relationship of heights.
<term>height</term>: the vertical distance (altitude) of the slope.
<term>perpendicular</term>: a line at a perfect 90-degree angle to a horizontal base.

### THEOREM V, PROPOSITION V

The times of descent along planes of different length, slope and height bear to one another a ratio which is equal to the product of the ratio of the lengths by the square root of the inverse ratio of their heights.

Draw the planes *AB* and *AC*, having different inclinations, lengths, and heights. My theorem then is that the ratio of the time of descent along *AC* to that along *AB* is equal to the product of the ratio of *AC* to *AB* by the square root of the inverse ratio of their heights <note>In modern notation, this states that the ratio of the times ($T_1/T_2$) equals $(L_1/L_2) \times \sqrt{H_2/H_1}$.</note>.

<note>The diagram shows a vertical line AD representing the total height. Point G lies on AD, marking the height of plane AB. Point D marks the height of plane AC. The lines AB and AC represent the two different paths of descent.</note>

Hence follows the theorem.

**SAGREDO.** Please allow me to interrupt the lecture for a moment in order that I may clear up an idea which just occurs to me; one which, if it involve no fallacy, suggests at least a freakish and <insert>[224]</insert> interesting circumstance, such as often occurs in nature and in the realm of necessary consequences.

If, from any point fixed in a horizontal plane, straight lines be drawn extending indefinitely in all directions, and if we imagine a point to move along each of these lines with constant speed, all starting from the fixed point at the same instant and moving with equal speeds, then it is clear that all of these moving points will lie upon the circumference of a circle which grows larger and larger, always having the aforesaid fixed point as its center; this circle spreads out in precisely the same manner as the little waves do in the case of a pebble allowed to drop into quiet water, where the impact of the stone starts the motion in all directions, while the point of impact remains the center of these ever-expanding circular waves. Now the answer to this question surprises me, for I am led by the preceding theorems to believe that these particles will always lie upon the circumference of a single circle, ever increasing in size as the particles recede farther and farther from the point at which their motion began. ### Theorem VII, Proposition VII

If the heights of two inclined planes are to each other in the same ratio as the squares of their lengths, bodies starting from rest will traverse these planes in equal times.

Take two planes of different lengths and different inclinations, AE and AB, whose heights are AF and AD: let AF be to AD as the square of AE is to the square of AB; then, I say, that a body, starting from rest at **A**, will traverse the planes AE and AB in equal times. 

From the vertical line, draw the horizontal parallel lines EF and DB, the latter cutting AE at G. Since the ratio of the heights FA to DA is equal to the ratio of the squares of the lengths EA to BA, and since the ratio of heights FA to DA is also equal to the ratio of the lengths EA to GA, it follows that the ratio of lengths EA to GA is equal to the ratio of the squares of EA to BA. 

<image-desc>Geometric diagram labeled Fig. 60. It shows a vertical line AF with an intermediate point D. A horizontal line extends from D to B and another from F to E. Two inclined lines, AB and AE, originate from point A. Line AB ends at B on the horizontal line DB. Line AE passes through the horizontal line DB at point G and ends at E on the horizontal line FE. The diagram illustrates the geometry of inclined planes for calculating descent times.</image-desc>

### THEOREM VIII, PROPOSITION VIII

The times of descent along all inclined planes which intersect one and the same vertical circle, either at its highest or lowest point, are equal to the time of fall along the vertical diameter; for those planes which fall short of this diameter the times are shorter; for planes which cut this diameter, the times are longer.

**Fig. 61**
<note>This diagram illustrates a vertical circle. Chords are drawn from the top (Point A) and bottom (Point B). The theorem proves that whether a ball rolls down the full vertical diameter AB or a shorter, tilted path like the chord DB, the time taken is identical.</note>

Let AB be the vertical diameter of a circle which touches the horizontal plane. It has already been proven that the times of descent along planes drawn from either end, A or B, to the circumference are equal. In order to show that the time of descent <insert>[227]</insert> <note>Page 227 of the standard National Edition.</note> along the plane DF which falls short of the diameter is shorter we may draw the plane DB which is both longer and less steeply inclined than DF; whence it follows that the time along DF is less than that along DB and consequently along AB. In like manner, it is shown that the time of descent along CO which cuts the diameter is greater: for it is both longer and less steeply inclined than CB. Hence follows the theorem.

### THEOREM IX, PROPOSITION IX

If from any point on a horizontal line two planes, inclined at any angle, are drawn, and if they are cut by a line which makes with them angles alternately equal to the angles between these planes and the horizontal, then the times required to traverse those portions of the plane cut off by the aforesaid line are equal.

### COROLLARY

From this and the preceding proposition, it is clear that the vertical distance covered by a <term>freely falling body|An object falling solely under the influence of gravity, without air resistance.</term>, after a preliminary fall, and during the time-interval required to traverse an inclined plane, is greater than the length of the inclined plane itself. However, it is less than the distance the body would have traversed on the inclined plane during an equal time if it had started from rest without that preliminary fall. 

For since we have just shown that bodies falling from an elevated point A will traverse the plane EC in Fig. 72 in a shorter time than the vertical EB, it is evident that the distance along EB which will be traversed during a time equal to the descent along EC will be less than the whole of EB. 

But now, in order to show that this vertical distance is greater than the length of the inclined plane EC, we refer to Fig. 70 <note>This refers to the diagram used in the previous theorem on page 203.</note> of the preceding theorem, in which the vertical length BG is traversed in the same time as BC after a preliminary fall through AB. That BG is greater than BC is shown as follows: since BE and FB are equal <insert>[235]</insert> while BA is less than BD, it follows that FB will bear to BA a greater ratio than EB bears to BD; and, **by addition of ratios** <note>original Latin: *componendo*; a mathematical operation where if $a:b = c:d$, then $(a+b):b = (c+d):d$.</note>, FA will bear to BA a greater ratio than ED to DB. 

However, FA:AB = GF:FB (since AF is a <term>mean proportional|A geometric mean; a value $x$ such that the ratio $a:x$ is equal to $x:b$.</term> between BA and AG) and in the same way ED:BD = CE:EB. Hence GB bears to BF a greater ratio than CB bears to BE; therefore, we conclude that GB is greater than BC.

### PROBLEM IV, PROPOSITION XVII

Given a vertical line and an <term>inclined plane|A slanted surface, like a ramp, used here to study how gravity affects objects moving at an angle.</term>, it is required to lay off a distance along the given plane which will be traversed by a body, after falling down the <term>perpendicular|A line standing at a right angle to the horizon; a perfectly vertical drop.</term>, in the same time-interval which is needed for this body to fall from rest through the given perpendicular.

Let AB be the vertical line and BE the inclined plane. The problem is to determine on BE a distance such that a body, after falling through AB, will traverse it in a time equal to that required to traverse the perpendicular AB itself, starting from rest.

<image-desc>A geometric diagram labeled "Fig. 73". It shows a right angle with a horizontal line AD and a vertical line AB meeting at point A. An inclined line segment DE originates at point D on the horizontal line and passes through point B on the vertical line, continuing down to point E. A point F is marked on the inclined segment between B and E. The points on the incline, in descending order from the top right, are D, B, F, and E.</image-desc>

Draw the horizontal AD and extend the plane until it meets this line in D. Lay off FB equal to BA; and choose the point E such that the ratio of distance BD to FD is the same as the ratio of FD to DE <note>original: "BD:FD =DF:DE"</note>. Then, I say, the time of descent along BE, after the fall through AB, is equal to the time of fall, starting from rest at A, through AB. 

For, if we assume that the length AB represents the time of fall through AB, then the time of fall through DB will be represented by the time DB; and since the ratio of BD to FD is equal to the ratio of FD to DE, it follows that FD will represent the time of descent along the entire plane DE, while BF represents the time through the portion BE starting from rest at D. But the time of descent along BE after the preliminary descent along DB is the same as that after a preliminary fall through AB. Hence the time of descent along BE after AB will be BF, which of course is equal to the time of fall through AB from rest at A. <note>original: "Q. E. F." (Quod erat faciendum) — "which was to be done."</note>

### PROBLEM VII, PROPOSITION XX

Given any distance whatever and a portion of it laid off from the point at which motion begins, it is required to find another portion which lies at the other end of the distance and which is traversed in the same time as the first given portion.

<image-desc>A vertical line (Figure 77) with points labeled C, D, E, A, and B from top to bottom. C is at the top, followed by D, then E, then A, and finally B at the bottom.</image-desc>
<margin>Fig. 77</margin>

Let the given distance be CB and let CD be that part of it which is laid off from the beginning of motion. It is required to find another part, at the end B, which is traversed in the same time as the assigned portion CD. Let BA be a mean proportional between BC and CD; also let CE be a <term>third proportional<note>A value (c) that completes a sequence such that a:b = b:c. Here, Galileo uses these geometric ratios to calculate the physical relationship between distances fallen and the time elapsed.</note></term> to BC and CA. Then, I say, EB will be the distance which, after fall from C, will be traversed in the same time as CD itself. For if we agree that CB shall represent the time through the entire distance CB, then BA (which, of course, is a mean proportional between BC and CD) will represent the time along CD; and since CA is a mean proportional between BC and CE, it follows that CA will be the time through CE; but the total length CB represents the time through the total distance CB. Therefore the difference BA will be the time along the difference of distances, EB, after falling from C; but this same BA was the time of fall through CD. Consequently the distances CD and EB are traversed, from rest at C, in equal times.

### PROBLEM VIII, PROPOSITION XXII

Suppose we are given two different lengths of time, and we also know the distance an object falls vertically from a state of rest during the shorter of these two times. Our task is to find the exact angle for a slope, starting from the top of that vertical path, so that the time it takes for an object to descend that slope is exactly equal to the longer of the two given times.

Let **A** represent the longer time-interval and **B** represent the shorter one. Let the line **CD** represent the distance of a

->Fig. 79<-

vertical fall, starting from rest, completed during time **B**. We are required to find a plane starting at point **C** with a slope such that an object will travel its full length in time **A**.

To do this, draw a line **CX** from point **C** to the horizontal level <note>The horizontal level is the imaginary line extending sideways from the bottom of the vertical drop.</note> of such a length that the ratio <note>original: "ratio"; the mathematical relationship between two quantities</note> of time **B** to time **A** is the same as the ratio of distance **CD** to distance **CX**. It is clear that **CX** is the specific plane we are looking for, which an object will descend in time **A**. This is because we have already demonstrated that the time spent descending an inclined plane compared to the time spent falling vertically through its height follows the same ratio as the length of the slope compared to its vertical height. Therefore, the time taken to travel along **CX** compared to the time taken to fall down **CD** is the same as the length of **CX** compared to the length of **CD**. This matches our original ratio for time-interval **A**.

Hence we can infer that, if, after descent along the inclined plane AC of the adjoining figure, the motion is continued along a horizontal line, such as CT, the distance traversed by a body, during a time equal to the time of fall through AC, will be exactly **twice** the distance AC. <note>This is a fundamental discovery: an object that reaches a certain speed through acceleration will, if it stops accelerating and maintains that speed, travel exactly twice the original distance in the same amount of time.</note> The argument here employed is the same as the preceding. For it is clear, since OE:EF = EF:EC, that FC measures the time of descent along CO. But, if the horizontal line TC which is twice as long as CA, be divided into two equal parts at V then this line must be extended indefinitely in the direction of X before it will intersect the line AE produced; and accordingly the ratio of the infinite length TX to the infinite length VX is the same as the ratio of the infinite distance VX to the infinite distance CX.

The same result may be obtained by another method of approach, namely, by returning to the same line of argument which was employed in the proof of the first proposition. Let us 
<insert>[243]</insert>
consider the triangle ABC, which, by lines drawn parallel to its base, represents for us a velocity increasing in proportion to the time; if these lines are infinite in number, just as the points in the line AC are infinite or as the number of instants in any interval of time is infinite, they will form the area of the triangle. <note>Galileo is using a precursor to calculus here. He imagines the total distance traveled as the "area" made up of an infinite number of speed measurements taken at every instant of time.</note> Let us now suppose that the maximum velocity attained—that represented by the line BC—to be continued, without acceleration and at constant value through another interval of time equal to the first. From these velocities will be built up, in a similar manner, the area of the parallelogram ADBC, which is twice that of the triangle ABC; accordingly the distance traversed with these velocities during any given interval of time will be <note>Because the rectangle (representing constant speed) has exactly twice the area of the triangle (representing increasing speed from rest), the distance covered at that top speed is exactly double the distance covered during the acceleration phase.</note>

<summary>Galileo demonstrates through geometry that an object moving at a constant speed—the maximum speed it reached while falling—will cover exactly twice the distance in the same amount of time as it did during its initial acceleration. This utilizes a visual proof comparing the area of a triangle (acceleration) to a rectangle (constant speed).</summary>

Furthermore we may remark that any velocity once imparted to a moving body will be rigidly maintained as long as the external causes of acceleration or retardation are removed, a condition which is found only on horizontal planes; for in the case of planes which slope downwards there is already present a cause of acceleration, while on planes sloping upward there is retardation; from this it follows that motion along a horizontal plane is **perpetual**; for, if the velocity be uniform, it cannot be diminished or slackened, much less destroyed. Further, although any velocity which a body may have acquired through natural fall is permanently maintained so far as **its own nature** <note>original Latin: "suapte natura"</note> is concerned, yet it must be remembered that if, after descent along a plane inclined downwards, the body is deflected to a plane inclined upward, there is already existing in this latter plane a cause of retardation; for in any such plane this same body is subject to a natural acceleration downwards. Accordingly we have here the **superposition** <note>The scientific principle where two different physical states or motions combine to act on a single object at the same time.</note> of two different states, namely, the velocity acquired during the preceding fall which if acting alone would carry the body at a uniform rate to infinity, and the velocity which results from a natural acceleration downwards common to all bodies. It seems altogether reasonable, therefore, if we wish to trace the future history of a body which has descended along some inclined plane and has been deflected along some plane inclined upwards, for us to assume...

### THEOREM XXI, PROPOSITION XXXII

If in a horizontal line any two points are chosen and if
through one of these points a line be drawn inclined towards
the other, and if from this other point a straight line is
drawn to the inclined line in such a direction that it cuts
off from the inclined line a portion equal to the distance
between the two chosen points on the horizontal line, then
the time of descent along the line so drawn is less than along
any other straight line drawn from the same point to the
same inclined line. Along other lines which make equal
angles on opposite sides of this line, the times of descent are
the same.

### SCHOLIUM

From the preceding it is possible to infer that the path of quickest descent <note>original Latin: *lationem omnium velocissimam*, literally "the swiftest of all motions."</note> from one point to another is not the shortest path, namely, a straight line, but the arc of a circle. <note>Galileo is famous for this assertion, though it was later proven by mathematicians like Bernoulli and Newton that the "Brachistochrone," or path of swiftest descent, is actually a curve called a cycloid, not a circular arc.</note> In the quadrant BAEC, having the side BC vertical, divide the arc AC into any number of equal parts, AD, DE, EF, FG, GC, and from C draw straight lines to the points A, D, E, F, G; 

<image-desc>Fig. 103: A geometric diagram showing a quadrant with its vertex at B. Point B is at the top left, A is at the top right, and C is at the bottom left. A circular arc connects A and C. Several chords are drawn from point C to points A, D, E, F, and G on the arc. A polygonal path is also shown, formed by segments AD, DE, EF, FG, and GC.</image-desc> 

draw also the straight lines AD, DE, EF, FG, GC. Evidently descent along the path ADC is quicker than along AC alone or along DC from rest at D. But a body, starting from rest at A, will traverse DC more quickly than the path ADC; while, if it starts from rest at A, it will traverse the path DEC in a shorter time than DC alone. Hence descent along the three chords, ADEC, will take less time than along the two chords ADC. Similarly, following descent along ADE, the time required to traverse EFC is less than that needed for EC alone. Therefore descent is more rapid along the four chords ADEFC than along the three ADEC. And finally a body, after descent along ADEF, will traverse the two chords, FGC, more quickly than FC alone. Therefore, along the five chords, ADEFGC, descent will be more rapid than along the four, ADEFC. Consequently, as the number of chords is increased, the time of descent is continually reduced, and the motion becomes swifter as the path approaches the shape of a circular arc.

**SALVIATI.** Once more, Simplicio is here on time; so let us without delay take up the question of motion. The text of our Author <note>Galileo refers to himself as "the Author" throughout the book, as he is reading from his own formal Latin treatise on mechanics.</note> is as follows:

## THE MOTION OF PROJECTILES

In the preceding pages we have discussed the properties of uniform motion <note>Movement at a constant speed in a straight line.</note> and of motion naturally accelerated <note>The way an object speeds up naturally as it falls toward the Earth.</note> along planes of all inclinations. I now propose to set forth those properties which belong to a body whose motion is compounded of two other motions, namely, one uniform and one naturally accelerated; these properties, well worth knowing, I propose to demonstrate in a rigid manner. This is the kind of motion seen in a moving projectile; its origin I conceive to be as follows:

Imagine any particle projected along a horizontal plane without friction; then we know, from what has been more fully explained in the preceding pages, that this particle will move along this same plane with a motion which is uniform and perpetual, provided the plane has no limits. But if the plane is limited and elevated, then the moving particle, which we imagine to be a heavy one, will on passing over the edge of the plane acquire, in addition to its previous uniform and perpetual motion, a downward propensity due to its own weight; so that the resulting motion which I call projection <note>original: "projectio"</note>, is compounded of one which is uniform and horizontal and of another which is vertical and naturally accelerated. <meta>This page continues the Fourth Day of the dialogue. Salviati is addressing the discrepancy between the "perfect" mathematical world of parabolas and the "imperfect" physical world where factors like air resistance and the Earth's curvature exist. He has just finished explaining that even great scientists like Archimedes made simplifying assumptions to prove their theories.</meta>

# THE TWO NEW SCIENCES OF GALILEO

If we wish to apply our proven conclusions to distances which, though finite, are very large, it is necessary for us to infer—on the basis of demonstrated truth—what correction must be made for the fact that our distance from the center of the earth is not really infinite, but merely very great in comparison with the small dimensions of our apparatus. <note>In theoretical physics of this time, gravity was often treated as if it acted in parallel lines (as if the Earth were flat and infinitely far away). Galileo is acknowledging that gravity actually pulls toward a central point because the Earth is a sphere.</note> The largest of these dimensions will be the range of our **projectiles**—and even here we need consider only the **artillery**—which, however great, will never exceed four of those miles of which four thousand separate us from the center of the earth. Since these paths terminate upon the surface of the earth, only very slight changes can take place in their **parabolic figure**, which, it is conceded, would be greatly altered if they were to terminate at the center of the earth.

As to the perturbation arising from the **resistance of the medium** <note>This is "air resistance." Galileo identifies this as a much bigger practical problem than the Earth's curvature.</note>, this is more considerable and does not, on account of its many forms, submit to fixed laws and exact description. Thus, if we consider only the resistance which the air offers to the motions studied by us, we shall see that it disturbs them all, and disturbs them in an infinite variety of ways corresponding to the infinite variety in the form, weight, and velocity of the **projectiles**. 

For as to **velocity**, the greater this is, the greater will be the resistance offered by the air; a resistance which will be greater as the moving bodies become <gloss>less dense</gloss> <note>original Italian: "men gravi," literally "less heavy," but used here to denote density or weight relative to size.</note>. So that although the falling body ought to be displaced—<gloss>accelerating continually</gloss> <note>original Italian: "andare accelerandosi."</note>—in proportion to the square of the duration of its motion, yet no matter how heavy the body, if it falls from a very considerable height, the resistance of the air will be such as to prevent any further increase in speed and will render the motion

->[276]<-

uniform. <note>Galileo is describing what we now call "terminal velocity"—the point where the upward push of air resistance equals the downward pull of gravity, so the object stops accelerating and falls at a constant speed.</note> In proportion as the moving body is <gloss>less dense</gloss>, this uniformity will be so much the more quickly attained and after a shorter fall. Even **horizontal motion** which, if no impediment were offered, would be uniform and constant, is altered by the resistance of the air and finally ceases; and here again, the <gloss>lighter</gloss> <note>original Italian: "più leggiero."</note> the body, the quicker the process. Of these <term>accidental properties</term> <note>original Italian: "accidenti." In the science of the time, "accidents" were non-essential characteristics (like air resistance) that interfered with the "essential" mathematical law.</note> of weight, of velocity, and also of <gloss>shape</gloss> <note>original Italian: "figura."</note>, infinite in number, it is not possible to give...

### THEOREM II, PROPOSITION II

When the motion of a body is the resultant of two uniform motions, one horizontal, the other perpendicular, the **square** <note>original: *potentia*. <image-desc>A geometric diagram labeled Fig. 109. It shows a right-angled triangle where the vertical side is labeled 'ab' (with 'a' at the top and 'b' at the bottom right) and the horizontal side is labeled 'bc' (with 'c' at the left and 'b' at the bottom right). Let us imagine any body urged by two uniform motions and let *ab* represent the vertical displacement, while *bc* represents the displacement which, in the same interval of time, takes place in a horizontal direction. If then the distances *ab* and *bc* are traversed, during the same time-interval, with uniform motions the corresponding momenta will be to each other as the distances *ab* and *bc* are to each other; but the body which is urged by these two motions describes the diagonal *ac*; its momentum is proportional to *ac*. Also the square of *ac* is equal to the sum of the squares of *ab* and *bc*. Hence the square of the resultant momentum is equal to the sum of the squares of the two momenta *ab* and *bc*. **Which was to be demonstrated.** <note>original Latin: *Q. E.
